**Quaternary prevention:** mitigate harm from overmedicalization and unnecessary interventions

Advise adequate free water intake + low-sodium diet
Regularly monitor serum lithium levels, renal function, and electrolytes

Serial ultrasound surveillance to monitor renal growth and resolution

**Progressive marrow failure, bulky symptomatic adenopathy, or B symptoms:** assess TP53, del(17p), and IGHV before selecting targeted therapy.
Update nonlive vaccines and screen for hepatitis B before anti-CD20 treatment.

algorithm.title: Evaluation of spirometry and flow-volume loops

nodes.text: Dyspnea or cough with exertion: obtain pre- and post-bronchodilator spirometry

**FEV1 increases >12% and >200 mL post-bronchodilator:** asthma confirmed
**FEV1/FVC normal or elevated with FVC <80%:** suspect pulmonary restriction
**Total lung capacity <80% on plethysmography:** restrictive lung disease confirmed
Initiate inhaled low-dose corticosteroid plus formoterol for persistent asthma
Prescribe short-acting beta-2 agonist (albuterol) 15 minutes prior to exercise

Track linear growth and bone age annually to ensure normal final adult height

n-16-n16b2-q035.boardCall: Postviral acute bilateral paraparesis + sensory level + urinary retention -> demyelinating lesion (transverse myelitis).
n-16-n16b2-q035.hinge: Acute ascending sensorimotor deficits with a clear sensory level and neurogenic urinary retention indicate transverse myelitis.
n-16-n16b2-q035.trap: Epidural abscess presents similarly with cord compression but requires fever, leukocytosis, or bacteremic risk factors.

A.clue: T2 hyperintense spinal cord inflammation
A.fit: Here: postviral acute bilateral leg weakness, T10 sensory level, urinary retention

B.clue: Pus collection in epidural space with fever
B.fit: Not here: afebrile patient without spinal tenderness or systemic infection
B.tempting: acute back pain and cord compression

C.clue: Slowly progressive intramedullary neoplasm
C.fit: Not here: acute 3-day onset following an upper respiratory infection

D.clue: Fluid-filled cavitation of spinal cord
D.fit: Not here: acute paraplegia rather than chronic cape-like sensory dissociation
D.tempting: spinal cord sensory and motor deficit

E.clue: Bony vertebral fracture compressing the cord
E.fit: Not here: young patient without major trauma, osteoporosis, or malignancy

nodes.text: A sensory level, bilateral weakness, and urinary retention suggest transverse myelitis from an intramedullary demyelinating lesion.
Obtain urgent contrast-enhanced spine MRI to distinguish inflammatory myelitis from cord compression.
**Cord compression on MRI:** obtain emergency spine surgery evaluation.
**Noncompressive inflammatory cord lesion:** give high-dose IV methylprednisolone after evaluating for infection.
**Severe deficits persist after pulse methylprednisolone:** initiate therapeutic plasma exchange.
Drain acute bladder retention; obtain brain MRI, CSF, and selected AQP4 and MOG antibody testing.

triggers.text: severe back pain that radiates down her legs
difficulty emptying her bladder
tingling and numbness that began in her feet
upper respiratory tract infection with nonproductive cough
Placement of a urinary catheter drains 1 L of clear urine

n-16-n16b2-q036.boardCall: Heroin overdose with obtundation -> severe bradypnea (RR 6), hypercapnia (PCO2 80), and hypoxemia (PO2 45).
n-16-n16b2-q036.hinge: Opioids suppress the brainstem respiratory drive, causing central bradypnea with severe hypoventilation and CO2 retention.
n-16-n16b2-q036.trap: Mild bradypnea or normocapnic choices underestimate the severity of hypoventilation in an obtunded overdose patient.

A.clue: Marked bradypnea with respiratory acidosis and hypoxemia
A.fit: Here: obtunded patient with heroin use presenting in severe hypoventilation

B.clue: Mild bradypnea with normal carbon dioxide
B.fit: Not here: obtundation and severe hypoventilation cause significant hypercapnia

C.clue: Normal respiratory rate with moderate hypercapnia
C.fit: Not here: opioid overdose directly suppresses central respiratory rate

D.clue: Normal respiratory rate with marked hypercapnia
D.fit: Not here: profound central opioid intoxication causes marked bradypnea

E.clue: Tachypnea producing acute respiratory alkalosis
E.fit: Not here: rapid respiratory rate contradicts opioid-induced central respiratory depression

nodes.text: Heroin suppresses brainstem respiratory drive, causing bradypnea, elevated arterial carbon dioxide, and low arterial oxygen.
**Apnea or ineffective breathing:** provide immediate bag-mask ventilation with oxygen.
Give IV or intranasal naloxone promptly and reassess ventilation.
**Inadequate ventilation after initial naloxone:** repeat naloxone and secure the airway if ventilation cannot be maintained.
**Recurrent hypoventilation or suspected long-acting opioid:** monitor longer and consider naloxone infusion.
Offer take-home naloxone and treatment for opioid use disorder.

triggers.text: unresponsive in the bathroom
used heroin in the past
blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg
obtunded and only responds to painful stimuli

n-16-n16b2-q037.boardCall: Preterm labor tocolytic trial with p=0.23 -> no statistically significant reduction in 48-hour delivery.
n-16-n16b2-q037.hinge: A p-value greater than 0.05 indicates the observed difference is not statistically significant, failing to prove benefit.
n-16-n16b2-q037.trap: A 4% absolute reduction (14% vs 10%) or 29% relative reduction cannot be concluded when p > 0.05.

A.clue: Misinterprets p-value as relative risk reduction
A.fit: Not here: p-value represents probability of type I error

B.clue: Inverts direction of effect and conflates p-value
B.fit: Not here: intervention group had fewer deliveries and nonsignificant p-value

C.clue: Calculates relative reduction without statistical significance
C.fit: Not here: p=0.23 exceeds alpha threshold of 0.05

D.clue: Erroneously claims increased delivery risk
D.fit: Not here: delivery rate was lower in the intervention arm

E.clue: Nonsignificant difference fails to reject null hypothesis
E.fit: Here: p=0.23 indicates no statistically significant difference from placebo

nodes.text: Formulate hypotheses: null hypothesis states no difference between intervention and control
Set significance threshold (alpha), typically 0.05
Compare study p-value to alpha threshold
**p < 0.05:** reject null hypothesis and conclude statistically significant difference
**p >= 0.05:** fail to reject null hypothesis; no significant difference demonstrated
Examine 95% confidence intervals to evaluate clinical precision and study power

triggers.text: contractions every 3 minutes that last 60 seconds
cervix is 4 cm dilated and 75% effaced; the vertex is at –1 station
10% of women in preterm labor who receive a tocolytic agent

n-16-n16b2-q038.boardCall: Athletic child with localized tenderness over enlarged tibial tuberosity -> enthesitis (Osgood-Schlatter).
n-16-n16b2-q038.hinge: Traction apophysitis at the patellar tendon insertion onto the tibial tubercle defines Osgood-Schlatter disease enthesitis.
n-16-n16b2-q038.trap: Tibial fracture or osteomyelitis cause acute severe pain and systemic features rather than chronic exertional apophyseal pain.

A.clue: Increased compartment pressure causing neurovascular compromise
A.fit: Not here: chronic exertional pain without paresthesia, pallor, or tenseness

B.clue: Inflammation at tendon-to-bone attachment site
B.fit: Here: 10-year-old athlete with point tenderness over enlarged tibial tubercle

C.clue: Cortical bone disruption from acute trauma
C.fit: Not here: gradual 1-month pain without trauma or inability to bear weight

D.clue: Subchondral bone avascular necrosis of femoral condyle
D.fit: Not here: anterior tibial tubercle localization rather than joint line pain

E.clue: Infection of bone cortex and marrow
E.fit: Not here: afebrile patient with chronic activity-related pain and no erythema

nodes.text: Activity-related tibial tubercle pain in a growing athlete suggests Osgood-Schlatter traction enthesitis.
Reduce painful jumping or running; use ice, short-term NSAIDs, and quadriceps and hamstring stretching.
**Acute trauma with inability to bear weight or extend the knee:** obtain radiographs for tibial tubercle avulsion.
**Fever or progressive pain at rest:** evaluate for infection with inflammatory markers and imaging.
**Pain limits walking despite activity modification:** consider brief immobilization and reassess the diagnosis.
Return to sport gradually as pain allows; symptoms generally resolve with skeletal maturity.

triggers.text: 1-month history of daily left knee pain
worse later in the day or with activity/running
relief with ice

n-16-n16b2-q039.boardCall: Calf tenderness + elevated D-dimer -> duplex ultrasonography of the lower extremities.
n-16-n16b2-q039.hinge: An elevated D-dimer in a patient with suspected deep venous thrombosis requires confirmation with duplex ultrasound.
n-16-n16b2-q039.trap: Empiric anticoagulation without ultrasound is premature when the patient is stable and diagnosis remains unconfirmed.

A.clue: First-line noninvasive imaging confirming venous thrombus
A.fit: Here: calf pain, tenderness, and elevated D-dimer require diagnostic confirmation

B.clue: Outdated test measuring venous volume changes
B.fit: Not here: duplex ultrasound has superior diagnostic sensitivity and specificity

C.clue: Inpatient parenteral anticoagulation for venous thrombosis
C.fit: Not here: anticoagulation is premature before ultrasound confirms presence of thrombus

D.clue: Subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin anticoagulation
D.fit: Not here: objective ultrasound confirmation required before starting therapeutic anticoagulation

E.clue: Direct oral factor Xa inhibitor anticoagulation
E.fit: Not here: empiric anticoagulation premature in low-risk patient before ultrasound

nodes.text: Calculate Wells score for deep venous thrombosis (DVT)
**Low pretest probability (Wells score <= 1):** check high-sensitivity D-dimer
**Negative D-dimer:** DVT ruled out; no further testing or anticoagulation
**Positive D-dimer:** obtain lower extremity duplex ultrasonography
**High pretest probability (Wells score >= 2):** obtain duplex ultrasonography directly
Confirm acute DVT: start therapeutic anticoagulation (apixaban, rivaroxaban, or LMWH)
**Contraindication to anticoagulation:** place retrievable IVC filter

triggers.text: right lower leg pain that began this morning and has become increasingly severe with walking
Examination of the right leg shows calf tenderness
There is no pedal edema
Serum D-dimer concentration is increased

n-16-n16b2-q040.boardCall: Pediatric generalized anxiety disorder refractory to therapy -> start SSRI (sertraline).
n-16-n16b2-q040.hinge: Persistent generalized anxiety disorder with functional impairment despite weekly psychotherapy requires first-line SSRI pharmacotherapy.
n-16-n16b2-q040.trap: Passive suicidal ideation without intent or plan does not warrant psychiatric hospitalization.

A.clue: Tricyclic antidepressant with anticholinergic and cardiotoxic adverse effects
A.fit: Not here: SSRIs are first-line pharmacotherapy with superior safety profile

B.clue: Short-acting benzodiazepine for acute panic episodes
B.fit: Not here: ineffective for chronic generalized anxiety and carries dependence risk

C.clue: Neuroimaging evaluating structural brain pathology
C.fit: Not here: normal physical examination without focal neurologic deficits

D.clue: Inpatient admission for imminent suicide risk
D.fit: Not here: passive suicidal thoughts without intent, plan, or acute safety risk

E.clue: First-line SSRI for pediatric generalized anxiety disorder
E.fit: Here: 6-month severe anxiety and depression refractory to weekly therapy

F.clue: Nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic for short-term insomnia
F.fit: Not here: does not treat core generalized anxiety disorder causing sleep disturbance

nodes.text: Screen for generalized anxiety disorder using standardized clinical rating scales
**Imminent suicide risk with active plan:** emergency psychiatric hospitalization
Mild anxiety: initiate cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)
Moderate-to-severe or CBT-refractory anxiety: initiate SSRI (sertraline or fluoxetine)
**Inadequate response after 8-12 weeks:** titrate dose or switch to alternative SSRI
Combine SSRI pharmacotherapy with ongoing cognitive behavioral therapy
Monitor closely for adverse effects and behavioral activation

triggers.text: 6-month history of worsening anxiety and depressed mood
my brain doesn't get a break
constant worry about her academic performance and safety of family members
sees a therapist weekly
suicidal thoughts but has no current plan to harm herself or others

abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.name: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.scope: screening recommendations (men 65-75 who smoked), ultrasound imaging, surveillance intervals, elective repair thresholds, rupture
abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.core: Older adult with abdominal aortic dilation may remain asymptomatic until expansion or rupture; sudden abdominal/back pain and hypotension require immediate vascular rescue.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking strongest modifiable risk; older age, male sex, family history, hypertension, atherosclerosis
Women have higher rupture risk at smaller diameters; most aneurysms infrarenal
Existing AAA: **diameter and high BP** predict rupture; cholesterol, A1c do not

rows.label: Clues
items: Incidental pulsatile expansile abdominal mass; localized persistent pain suggests symptomatic aneurysm
Rupture triad incompletely present; transient stability may reflect contained retroperitoneal hemorrhage
Blue toe/distal ischemia may result from mural thrombus embolization
Acute back pain unchanged by movement = **referred pain**; prevertebral calcification on x-ray; not disc disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Medial elastin/collagen degradation → progressive enlargement; greater wall radius increases tension

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal ultrasound** diagnoses AAA, generally diameter ≥3 cm; no contrast required
★ Stable suspected rupture or preoperative planning → **CT angiography**
Unstable suspected rupture → bedside ultrasound if immediate; no CT transport delaying surgery
Ultrasound detects aneurysm but cannot reliably exclude rupture; follow symptoms/hemodynamics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Rupture → **urgent vascular repair**, IV access, blood products; avoid delaying for complete workup
Permissive hypotension during transfer/resuscitation until hemorrhage control when clinically feasible
★ Elective repair: **≥5.5 cm men, ≥5.0 cm women**, symptoms; **not if short life expectancy** (metastatic cancer)
Rapid growth ≥0.5 cm/6 months → repair consideration; endovascular versus open based on anatomy/fitness
Smaller asymptomatic lesions → ultrasound surveillance below; refer vascular surgery, manage cardiovascular risks

rows.label: Complications
items: Rupture, thrombosis, distal embolization; repair → AKI, bowel ischemia, endoleak after EVAR
Aortoenteric fistula after prior graft: herald GI bleed → catastrophic hemorrhage; urgent evaluation

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ USPSTF: **one-time ultrasound men 65–75 who ever smoked**; selectively screen never-smoking men
Women never smoked/no family history → no screening; women smokers/family history → USPSTF evidence insufficient
Smoking cessation, BP control, statin for atherosclerotic disease; lifelong imaging follow-up after EVAR

rows.label: Mimics
items: Renal colic: flank-to-groin pain, hematuria; shock atypical
Aortic dissection: abrupt chest/back pain, possible pulse deficits or branch ischemia

acetaminophen-toxicity.name: Acetaminophen toxicity
acetaminophen-toxicity.scope: Rumack-Matthew nomogram, 4-hour post-ingestion level, toxic metabolite NAPQI, N-acetylcysteine indications and timing, acute liver failure
acetaminophen-toxicity.core: Potentially toxic acetaminophen ingestion can be asymptomatic initially; time-specific concentration and hepatic injury determine immediate N-acetylcysteine treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Intentional overdose, repeated excessive dosing, unrecognized combination cold/pain products
Malnutrition and chronic heavy alcohol use increase vulnerability, especially with repeated supratherapeutic use
Extended-release products and opioid/anticholinergic co-ingestion may delay absorption

rows.label: Clues
items: First day: nausea/vomiting or no symptoms; next 1–3 days: RUQ pain, rising AST/ALT
★ **Coagulopathy, hypoglycemia, encephalopathy**, acidosis → severe hepatic failure
Early normal transaminases and clinical improvement do not establish safety

rows.label: Pathophys
items: CYP metabolism produces NAPQI; glutathione depletion → centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis
N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and benefits established liver failure beyond toxin clearance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Known acute ingestion → **acetaminophen concentration at ≥4 hours**; earlier result cannot risk-stratify
★ Plot **Rumack–Matthew nomogram**, 4–24 h; treatment line starts 150 µg/mL at 4 h
Unknown timing/repeated supratherapeutic use → no nomogram; obtain concentration, AST/ALT, INR, glucose, creatinine
Delayed absorption and initial detectable subthreshold level → repeat concentration after 4–6 h
Assess co-ingestions/pregnancy; intentional ingestion → psychiatric safety evaluation after stabilization

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ At/above treatment line → **N-acetylcysteine**, ideally within 8 h; benefit persists when delayed
Likely substantial ingestion and result delayed beyond 8 h → start antidote while awaiting testing
Unknown time: >10 µg/mL or liver injury; repeated excess: ≥20 µg/mL or abnormal aminotransferases → treat
Recent acute overdose, protected airway → activated charcoal, usually within 4 h; toxicology consultation
Continue antidote until clearance and hepatic/coagulation recovery criteria met; acute liver failure → transplant center

rows.label: Complications
items: Fulminant hepatic failure, AKI, cerebral edema, hypoglycemia, death
IV antidote → non-IgE-mediated infusion reaction; pause/treat reaction, then resume when needed

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Count acetaminophen across all products**, avoid duplicate dosing, secure storage
Assess suicide risk and arrange mental-health care after deliberate ingestion

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ischemic hepatitis: preceding profound hypotension
Viral hepatitis: exposure/serology without toxic ingestion pattern

acid-base-disorders.name: Acid-base disorders
acid-base-disorders.scope: Metabolic acidosis (anion gap, non-anion gap), metabolic alkalosis (saline-responsive vs saline-resistant), respiratory acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, Winter formula, mixed disorders
acid-base-disorders.core: Identify the primary pH disturbance, test expected compensation, then investigate the anion gap or urine chloride to locate the cause.

rows.label: Definition
items: Acidemia: pH <7.35; alkalemia: >7.45; normal pH can hide opposing primary disorders
Metabolic: primary HCO3 change; respiratory: primary PaCO2 change

rows.label: Formula
items: ★ **AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3)**; usual normal ≈8–12, laboratory dependent
Hypoalbuminemia correction: add 2.5 to AG per 1 g/dL albumin below 4
★ **Winter: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ±2**

rows.label: Interpret
items: HCO3 12 → expected PaCO2 26 ±2; measured 40 → additional respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis: expected PaCO2 ≈40 + 0.7 × (HCO3 − 24), ±5
Respiratory HCO3 change per 10 PaCO2: acidosis +1 acute/+4 chronic; alkalosis −2 acute/−4 chronic

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ Alkalosis: **urine Cl <20 mmol/L** → saline-responsive; ≥20 → diuretics/mineralocorticoids
ΔAG exceeds HCO3 fall → additional alkalosis; smaller ΔAG → additional non-gap acidosis

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Compensation never overshoots; values outside expected range imply **mixed disorder**
Salicylates often cause respiratory alkalosis plus high-gap acidosis; near-normal pH is deceptive
Diarrhea/RTA: non-gap acidosis; distal RTA: urine pH >5.5, hypokalemia; renal failure: either gap pattern

acid-base-disorders.evidence: Established physiologic formulas; no guideline involved.

acute-leukemias.name: Acute leukemias
acute-leukemias.scope: Acute myeloid leukemia, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute promyelocytic leukemia, bone marrow biopsy, Auer rods
acute-leukemias.core: Rapid marrow replacement produces cytopenias and circulating immature cells; acute promyelocytic leukemia with coagulopathy demands immediate treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior cytotoxic treatment/radiation, benzene, myelodysplasia → AML
Down syndrome increases childhood leukemia risk; ALL predominates in children

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, fever/infections, bruising, bone pain; WBC may be high, normal or low
Hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy; T-ALL → mediastinal mass and airway/SVC compression
★ Bleeding with prolonged PT, low fibrinogen → suspect **APL-associated DIC**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Clonal immature myeloid or lymphoid expansion displaces normal hematopoiesis
Blast differentiation arrest; cell turnover predisposes to urate/phosphate release

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC/differential and smear → bone marrow biopsy**, flow cytometry, cytogenetics
Usually ≥20% marrow/blood blasts; defining genetic abnormalities permit some AML diagnoses below threshold
BMP, uric acid, LDH, coagulation profile; lumbar puncture for ALL CNS evaluation after stabilization

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected APL → **ATRA immediately**, then arsenic trioxide-based regimen; correct coagulopathy aggressively
Febrile neutropenia → IV cefepime; symptomatic cytopenias → blood-product support
AML → cytarabine/daunorubicin; less-fit adults → azacitidine/venetoclax; selected patients → allogeneic transplant
ALL → vincristine/steroid/asparaginase-based chemotherapy + intrathecal methotrexate; BCR-ABL-positive → add imatinib
★ Tumor-lysis prevention → hydration/allopurinol; high risk → **rasburicase**, contraindicated with G6PD deficiency

rows.label: Complications
items: Leukostasis: respiratory distress/confusion → urgent cytoreduction; tumor lysis → AKI, arrhythmias
Treatment → opportunistic infection, infertility, cardiomyopathy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Leukemoid reaction: mature neutrophilia with toxic granulation, reactive trigger
Aplastic anemia: hypocellular marrow without blast expansion

acute-leukemias.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

adolescent-confidentiality-and-care.name: Adolescent confidentiality and care
adolescent-confidentiality-and-care.scope: Confidentiality principles, exceptions to parental notification, parental requests for drug testing, encouraging family involvement
adolescent-confidentiality-and-care.core: Provide adolescents private, developmentally appropriate care; explain confidentiality and its safety limits before sensitive questions.

rows.label: Principle
items: Confidentiality supports honest disclosure; consent authority and parental access vary by jurisdiction
Assent: involve the adolescent even when guardian permission remains necessary
Contraception: minors generally consent confidentially; no parental notice or pelvic exam required

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Interview alone** for sexual health, substance use, mood, violence, and safety
★ Explain permitted confidential services; protect portals, billing, and result notifications
Encourage trusted-adult involvement; never require disclosure for legally confidential services

rows.label: Don't
items: ★ Parental request for **drug testing** → discuss concern, interview teen; avoid covert testing
Do not promise absolute secrecy or automatically send sensitive findings to parents
Do not breach for experimental substance use without impairment → counsel, schedule **follow-up visit**

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Imminent danger, suspected **abuse/neglect/exploitation** → protective disclosure and reporting
Emergency treatment when delay risks serious harm; involve guardians when feasible
Emancipated minors generally self-consent; pregnancy alone does not universally confer emancipation

rows.label: Traps
items: Minor consent varies: STI, contraception, pregnancy, mental health, substance; **elective surgery** → parents
Mandatory reporting thresholds for consensual sexual activity depend on ages and local law
Disclose minimum necessary information; explain safety-driven disclosure to adolescent whenever feasible

adolescent-confidentiality-and-care.evidence: Not checked online; established ethics principles; jurisdiction-specific consent/reporting law must be verified locally.

airway-management.name: Airway management
airway-management.scope: Indications for endotracheal intubation (GCS <= 8, airway protection, respiratory failure), rapid sequence intubation, bag-valve-mask ventilation, difficult airway
airway-management.core: Secure the airway when oxygenation, ventilation, or protection fails; preparation and rescue oxygenation determine safety.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Facial/neck trauma, burns, angioedema, obesity, limited jaw opening or cervical mobility
Shock, severe hypoxemia, metabolic acidosis increase peri-intubation collapse risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **GCS ≤8**, absent protective reflexes, recurrent aspiration, apnea → assess need for definitive airway
Stridor, fatigue, rising CO₂, refractory hypoxemia, inability to handle secretions → impending failure
GCS alone imperfect: reversible intoxication without ventilation/protection failure may permit closely monitored observation
Toxic sore throat, drooling, stridor → epiglottitis: laryngoscopy + intubation in OR before imaging/cultures

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Upper-airway obstruction, depressed drive, or respiratory muscle failure prevents effective gas exchange
Induction/positive pressure reduces sympathetic tone and venous return, worsening hypotension

rows.label: Dx
items: Continuous pulse oximetry, ECG, BP; assess mouth opening, neck anatomy, aspiration risk
★ Confirm tracheal placement with **persistent waveform capnography**, then auscultation and chest radiograph for depth
Do not rely on chest movement, oxygen saturation, or auscultation alone

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Position, suction, **preoxygenate**; prepare BVM, supraglottic device, video laryngoscope, and surgical rescue
Two-person BVM with airway adjunct and oxygen; oral adjunct only without gag reflex
RSI: etomidate/ketamine + rocuronium/succinylcholine; provide immediate postintubation analgesia and sedation
★ Predicted difficult airway → awake intubation strategy; **cannot intubate/cannot oxygenate or shattered midface/mandible → cricothyrotomy**
Avoid succinylcholine: hyperkalemia, denervation, established major burns, neuromuscular disease, malignant hyperthermia risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Esophageal intubation, aspiration, dental injury, hypoxemia, cardiac arrest
Positive-pressure ventilation → barotrauma; prolonged ventilation → pneumonia, laryngeal injury
Right-mainstem tube → occludes right upper lobe bronchus → **alveolar collapse** (atelectasis), not air trapping
Prolonged intubation → **tracheomalacia**: dynamic expiratory collapse, localized wheeze, exertional dyspnea; not asthma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Optimize **hemodynamics before induction**, use attempt limits and explicit backup plan
Head-of-bed elevation, oral care, daily sedation/ventilator liberation assessment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic hyperventilation: preserved oxygenation/protection, respiratory alkalosis
Compensatory Kussmaul breathing: metabolic acidosis; losing minute ventilation can cause abrupt deterioration

airway-management.evidence: Not checked online; established emergency airway principles.

anaphylaxis.name: Anaphylaxis
anaphylaxis.scope: Anaphylaxis, angioedema, biphasic reactions, epinephrine autoinjector, emergency airway management
anaphylaxis.core: Rapid multisystem reaction after exposure—or isolated hypotension or airway compromise after a known allergen—requires epinephrine immediately.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Foods, insect venom, antibiotics, latex; exercise can amplify food-triggered reactions
Asthma, prior severe reaction, mast-cell disorders; beta-blockers can complicate treatment

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Urticaria/angioedema + wheeze, stridor, hypotension, or severe GI symptoms**
Skin findings may be absent; hoarseness and tongue swelling predict airway danger
Biphasic recurrence after apparent resolution, especially after severe or undertreated episodes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mast-cell/basophil mediators → vasodilation, capillary leak, bronchoconstriction; often IgE-mediated
Epinephrine: α1 reverses vasodilation/edema, β2 reverses bronchoconstriction; albuterol alone misses edema and shock

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; never wait for tryptase or laboratory confirmation
Acute and baseline serum tryptase can support uncertain cases; normal results do not exclude anaphylaxis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg**, adult 0.3–0.5 mg, lateral thigh; repeat every 5–15 minutes
Supine with legs elevated unless respiratory distress; oxygen, early intubation for progressive obstruction
Profound shock or refractory hypotension → titrated IV epinephrine plus **isotonic boluses**; beta-blocker use → glucagon
Albuterol for residual bronchospasm; antihistamines relieve itching only; steroids do not reliably prevent biphasic reactions
★ Monitor until resolved; **longer observation/admission** after hypotension, repeated epinephrine, or severe asthma

rows.label: Complications
items: Asphyxia, distributive shock, arrhythmia, hypoxic brain injury
Undiluted IV epinephrine bolus errors → ischemia and dangerous dysrhythmia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Prescribe **epinephrine autoinjector**, demonstrate technique, provide written action plan and allergy referral
Extra device for repeat-dose risk; avoidance, medical alert ID; venom immunotherapy after qualifying sting allergy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vasovagal episode: bradycardia, pallor, rapid improvement supine
Bradykinin angioedema: no itching/hives; ACE inhibitor or hereditary disease → airway, icatibant/C1 inhibitor

ankle-and-foot-injuries.name: Ankle and foot injuries
ankle-and-foot-injuries.scope: Lateral ankle sprain, Ottawa ankle and foot rules, RICE therapy, functional rehabilitation, Achilles tendon rupture, plantar fasciitis, calcaneal apophysitis
ankle-and-foot-injuries.core: Mechanism, focal tenderness, weight-bearing ability, and tendon function distinguish ankle sprain from fracture and overuse foot disorders.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Inversion while plantarflexed, prior sprain, poor balance → lateral ligament injury
Running/jumping, sudden training increase, tight calves, obesity; fluoroquinolones/steroids increase tendon rupture risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Lateral swelling after inversion → **anterior talofibular ligament** injury most likely
Pain above ankle with external rotation/squeeze → syndesmotic sprain; recovery slower
Focal bony pain, deformity, neurovascular changes, or inability to bear weight → fracture evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ligament overstretch → microtears or disruption; tendon degeneration predisposes rupture
Repeated loading damages soft tissue; tendon degeneration reduces tensile strength

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Ankle pain + **posterior-edge/tip malleolar tenderness** → ankle radiographs
★ Midfoot pain + **navicular or fifth-metatarsal-base tenderness** → foot radiographs
Either region: inability to take four steps immediately and during evaluation also triggers corresponding radiographs
Examine skin, pulses, sensation; persistent focal pain despite normal films → reassess occult fracture

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Sprain: **protection, ice, compression, elevation**, brief analgesia; early protected weight-bearing
Functional brace + range-of-motion, strength, proprioceptive rehabilitation; avoid prolonged routine immobilization
Displaced/open fracture or neurovascular compromise → urgent orthopedics; immobilize and keep non-weight-bearing

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic instability, recurrent sprains, osteochondral talar injury
Missed syndesmotic injury → prolonged disability; immobilization → stiffness, thrombosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Balance training and bracing** after prior sprain; gradual return when strength/function restored
Gradual training progression, supportive footwear, calf flexibility; avoid premature athletic return

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lisfranc injury: plantar ecchymosis, midfoot instability; weight-bearing radiographs
Septic arthritis: fever, marked passive-motion pain; aspirate joint

table.title: Heel disorders
rows: Pop, weak plantarflexion, abnormal Thompson test
First-step morning pain; medial plantar heel
Active child; posterior heel squeeze tenderness

ankle-and-foot-injuries.evidence: Not checked online; established orthopedic decision rules and rehabilitation principles.

antepartum-bleeding.name: Antepartum bleeding
antepartum-bleeding.scope: Placenta previa, placental abruption, vasa previa, uterine rupture, transabdominal ultrasound before digital exam, Kleihauer-Betke test, emergent cesarean delivery
antepartum-bleeding.core: Bleeding in later pregnancy requires immediate maternal stabilization and fetal assessment, followed by placental localization before any digital cervical examination.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Previa: prior cesarean, multiparity; abruption: hypertension, cocaine, trauma, prior abruption
Vasa previa: velamentous cord, accessory placental lobe, IVF; rupture: uterine scar, obstructed labor

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Shock may exceed visible blood loss** with concealed abruption or internal hemorrhage
Assess uterine tone, pain, contractions, fetal tracing, membrane status; bleeding volume alone is unreliable

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Maternal placental bleeding versus fetal vessel hemorrhage; vasa previa can rapidly exsanguinate fetus
Placental separation or uterine disruption compromises oxygen delivery independent of maternal external blood loss

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ CBC, type/crossmatch, coagulation studies including fibrinogen; continuous fetal monitoring if viable
★ **Ultrasound before digital examination**; transabdominal first; transvaginal safely clarifies placenta–cervix relationship
Normal ultrasound does not exclude abruption; suspected rupture is a clinical emergency
Rh-negative bleeding/trauma → Kleihauer–Betke or flow cytometry quantifies fetomaternal hemorrhage for anti-D dosing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ ABCs, two large IVs, blood products when needed; **do not delay delivery for imaging if unstable**
Hemorrhage/fetal compromise → emergency cesarean; rupture → laparotomy, uterine repair or hysterectomy
Stable preterm previa → observation, pelvic rest, corticosteroids when eligible; planned cesarean before labor
Abruption: deliver if significant or compromised; vaginal birth possible when stable and imminent or fetal demise
Unsensitized Rh-negative patient → anti-D immunoglobulin; correct abruption-associated coagulopathy

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhagic shock, DIC, AKI, hysterectomy; fetal hypoxia, death, prematurity
Previa plus cesarean scar increases placenta accreta spectrum risk and operative hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Control BP, avoid cocaine/tobacco; prenatal placental/cord localization and planned high-risk delivery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Bloody show: small mucus-streaked bleeding with cervical change
Cervical lesion: contact bleeding, visible source on speculum examination

table.title: Critical distinctions
rows: Bleeding after rupture; sudden fetal bradycardia
Scarred uterus; sudden pain, lost station, fetal bradycardia

antepartum-bleeding.evidence: Not checked online; established obstetric hemorrhage teaching.

antidepressants.name: Antidepressants
antidepressants.scope: SSRIs, SNRIs, bupropion, mirtazapine, tricyclic antidepressants (anticholinergic toxicity, urinary retention, arrhythmia), MAO inhibitors, adverse effects (serotonin syndrome)
antidepressants.core: SSRIs usually start depression treatment; choose alternatives by accompanying symptoms, adverse effects, and overdose risk.

rows.label: Use
items: SSRIs/SNRIs: depression, anxiety; duloxetine also neuropathic pain
Bupropion: smoking cessation; mirtazapine: poor appetite with insomnia
TCAs/MAOIs: resistant depression; TCAs also neuropathic pain

rows.label: Mechanism
items: SSRIs: serotonin reuptake blockade; SNRIs/TCAs: serotonin + norepinephrine reuptake blockade
Bupropion: norepinephrine/dopamine reuptake blockade; mirtazapine: α2 antagonism
MAOIs: reduced monoamine degradation

rows.label: Adverse
items: SSRIs: GI upset, SIADH, bleeding; SNRIs: ↑BP; mirtazapine: sedation/weight gain; bupropion: activating
★ SSRI **sexual dysfunction** → **lower dose** first; other SSRIs rarely help; bupropion minimal
TCAs: constipation, urinary retention, conduction toxicity; MAOIs: orthostatic hypotension

rows.label: Avoid
items: ★ Bupropion lowers seizure threshold: **seizure or eating disorders**; CYP inhibitors raise levels
TCAs: urinary retention, glaucoma, conduction disease; anticholinergic delirium in older adults
TCA therapy with QTc/QRS prolongation → **stop TCA**, no waiting for levels

rows.label: Interactions
items: MAOI + tyramine/sympathomimetics → hypertensive crisis → **phentolamine** (α-blocker)
MAOI + SSRI/tramadol → serotonin syndrome; washout generally 14 days, after fluoxetine 5 weeks
Fluoxetine/paroxetine inhibit CYP2D6 → ↑TCA levels, toxicity

rows.label: Monitor
items: Mood, suicidality early in young adults; monitor adherence and functioning
Abrupt stop → **discontinuation**: flu-like aches, headache, dizziness, electric paresthesias, nausea, tremor
Response over 4–6 weeks; taper to stop, especially paroxetine and venlafaxine

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Serotonin syndrome**: clonus, fever/agitation → stop drugs, benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine
★ TCA overdose: Na⁺-channel blockade → **wide QRS**, arrhythmia, seizures → IV sodium bicarbonate
Bipolar depression: antidepressant monotherapy may provoke mania

antidepressants.evidence: Not checked online; established pharmacology and prescribing safety.

antipsychotics.name: Antipsychotics
antipsychotics.scope: First-generation vs second-generation, extrapyramidal symptoms (acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia), neuroleptic malignant syndrome, metabolic syndrome, hyperprolactinemia, QTc prolongation
antipsychotics.core: Dopamine-modulating drugs treat psychosis and mania; selection depends on motor, metabolic, endocrine, cardiovascular, and hematologic risks.

rows.label: Use
items: ★ Psychosis, mania, agitation; **SGA first-line**; **clozapine** if resistant or recurrent suicidality
FGA: mainly D2 antagonism; SGA: D2/5-HT2 effects, varying by agent
Quetiapine sedation → switch to aripiprazole; obesity → ziprasidone, not olanzapine/clozapine

rows.label: Mechanism
items: Nigrostriatal blockade → movement disorders; tuberoinfundibular blockade → prolactin elevation
Aripiprazole: partial D2 agonist; haloperidol high-potency FGA, chlorpromazine low-potency FGA
Chronic D2 blockade → receptor supersensitivity → tardive dyskinesia; can worsen after stopping

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ Fever, **lead-pipe rigidity**, autonomic instability, high CK → NMS; stop drug, supportive ICU care
Severe NMS: dantrolene/bromocriptine; olanzapine/clozapine: weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidemia
Risperidone: ↑prolactin; ziprasidone: ↑QT; clozapine: neutropenia, myocarditis, ileus, seizures

rows.label: Avoid
items: Lewy body/Parkinson disease: severe sensitivity; specialist-selected quetiapine/clozapine if essential
Dementia: ↑mortality, falls; dangerous behavior after safer measures → low-dose **quetiapine**/risperidone, not benzodiazepines

rows.label: Interactions
items: Other QT-prolonging drugs, electrolyte depletion → torsades; sedatives/alcohol increase CNS depression
Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine block dopamine: same EPS, tardive dyskinesia, NMS; avoid after NMS

rows.label: Monitor
items: ★ Weight/BMI, BP, glucose/A1c, lipids; movement examinations; **ANC with clozapine**
ECG for cardiac/QT risks; prolactin when symptomatic; ask about bowel function
Clozapine + ANC <1000 → **hold clozapine**, not dose reduction; ANC 1000–1499 → continue, closer monitoring

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Anticholinergics worsen tardive dyskinesia**; valbenazine/deutetrabenazine are VMAT2 inhibitors
Akathisia can mimic worsening agitation; increasing antipsychotic dose can worsen it
Low-potency FGAs: more orthostasis/anticholinergic effects; high-potency FGAs: more EPS

table.title: Extrapyramidal syndromes
rows: Stop/switch culprit first; benztropine or amantadine

antipsychotics.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [FDA clozapine monitoring update](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-removes-risk-evaluation-and-mitigation-strategy-rems-program-antipsychotic-drug-clozapine); other effects established teaching.

asthma.name: Asthma
asthma.scope: Diagnosis, stepwise therapy, acute exacerbation, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction
asthma.core: Variable episodes of wheeze, cough, dyspnea, and chest tightness from reversible expiratory airflow limitation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: **Family history of asthma/atopy**: strongest childhood risk; allergens, viral infections, smoke, occupational sensitizers
Exercise/cold air, aspirin-sensitive disease, nonselective beta-blockers; assess workplace symptom pattern

rows.label: Clues
items: Nocturnal/early-morning symptoms; normal examination between attacks
★ **Silent chest, exhaustion, altered mentation, rising PaCO2** → impending respiratory failure
Acute attack: low peak flow, accessory-muscle use, difficulty speaking
Cough-variant: isolated chronic cough, worse with cold/exercise; normal examination and radiograph

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Allergen cross-links IgE on **mast cells** → histamine, leukotrienes → bronchoconstriction
Airway inflammation, smooth-muscle constriction, mucus → variable obstruction and hyperresponsiveness
Persistent uncontrolled inflammation → remodeling with incompletely reversible airflow limitation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Spirometry**: obstruction with bronchodilator FEV1 increase >12% and >200 mL in adults
Normal spirometry with suspicion → repeat during symptoms or methacholine challenge
Exercise challenge: postexercise FEV1 fall >10%; assess baseline control before isolated exercise diagnosis
PFT pattern: ↓FEV1, normal/↓FVC, normal/↑TLC from air trapping

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Exacerbation → **repeated inhaled albuterol + ipratropium**, oxygen, early systemic glucocorticoids
Severe poor response → IV magnesium; deterioration → intubation; avoid sedatives and routine antibiotics
Exercise symptoms → preexercise albuterol or prescribed ICS-formoterol; persistent symptoms → improve controller
Check technique/adherence before stepping up; uncontrolled despite high-dose ICS-LABA → phenotype-directed biologic referral
Discharge: **PEF ≥70–80% predicted** (less wheeze is unreliable) + 5–7 day **oral prednisone** prevents relapse

rows.label: Complications
items: Status asthmaticus, pneumothorax, respiratory arrest
ICS → thrush/dysphonia; systemic steroids → osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, adrenal suppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Written action plan, trigger reduction, smoking cessation, spacer; rinse mouth after ICS
★ GINA: **no SABA-only treatment**, no LABA monotherapy; ICS with every reliever use
Older exam questions (NAEPP) may expect: symptoms ≤2 days/week, awakenings ≤2/month → **SABA alone**; more → daily ICS

rows.label: Mimics
items: Inducible laryngeal obstruction: inspiratory stridor, inspiratory flow-loop flattening
COPD: persistent obstruction, smoking history
HF: edema, elevated JVP, cardiac findings
Deconditioning: obese/sedentary, exertional dyspnea; normal PFTs, no bronchodilator response

atopic-dermatitis.name: Atopic dermatitis
atopic-dermatitis.scope: Atopic dermatitis, pruritus, flexural lichenification, emollients and topical corticosteroids, complications (eczema herpeticum, bacterial infection)
atopic-dermatitis.core: Chronic relapsing itchy eczema with xerosis; infants often have facial/extensor disease, while older children develop flexural lichenification.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Personal/family atopy, impaired skin barrier, dry climate; soaps, wool, fragrances, heat can trigger flares
Asthma and allergic rhinitis commonly coexist; scratching and bacterial colonization exacerbate inflammation

rows.label: Clues
items: Excoriations, erythema, oozing during flares; sleep disturbance and chronic thickening from rubbing
★ **Painful monomorphic punched-out erosions**, fever, rapid spread → eczema herpeticum
Honey-colored crusts, pustules, warmth or spreading erythema → secondary bacterial infection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Barrier dysfunction increases water loss and allergen penetration; type 2 inflammation drives itch–scratch cycle

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis** by itch, distribution, chronicity; no routine serum IgE/food allergy panels
Atypical/refractory disease → assess contact allergy, infestation, immune deficiency; selected patch testing
Suspected HSV complication → lesion PCR, but begin treatment before results if clinically convincing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Daily **thick emollient**, short lukewarm bathing, fragrance-free cleanser; apply moisturizer promptly afterward
★ Flares → **topical corticosteroid**, potency by site/severity: triamcinolone on body; hydrocortisone on face/folds
Tacrolimus/pimecrolimus for sensitive sites or steroid-sparing maintenance; wet wraps for selected severe flares
Refractory moderate/severe disease → phototherapy or dupilumab; avoid chronic systemic glucocorticoids
★ Eczema herpeticum → **systemic acyclovir** now; ocular involvement → ophthalmology

rows.label: Complications
items: S aureus superinfection, disseminated HSV, sleep loss, psychosocial burden
Excess topical steroid potency/duration → skin atrophy, striae; dupilumab → conjunctivitis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Barrier care, trigger reduction, short nails; intermittent maintenance anti-inflammatory treatment at recurrent sites
No empiric elimination diets without confirmed clinical allergy; avoid routine antibiotics for uninfected eczema

rows.label: Mimics
items: Contact dermatitis: exposure-shaped distribution, patch-test association
Scabies: nocturnal household itch, burrows in webs/wrists
Seborrheic dermatitis: greasy scale, less itching

atrial-fibrillation.name: Atrial fibrillation
atrial-fibrillation.scope: Rate and rhythm control, stroke prevention (CHA2DS2-VASc), unstable AF, embolic complications
atrial-fibrillation.core: Disorganized atrial activation produces an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm and left atrial appendage thromboembolism risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, hypertension, heart failure, coronary disease, obesity, sleep apnea
Hyperthyroidism, alcohol binges, infection, postoperative stress, mitral valve disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Palpitations, exercise intolerance, dyspnea; sometimes incidental or first detected after stroke
★ **Hypotension, ischemic chest pain, pulmonary edema, altered mentation** → unstable AF
Very rapid irregular wide-complex rhythm suggests preexcitation; ordinary AV nodal blockers can be dangerous

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pulmonary-vein ectopic triggers plus atrial remodeling sustain reentry
Loss of atrial contraction reduces filling; persistent tachycardia can impair LV function

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG: absent discrete P waves**, variable RR intervals; document rhythm rather than pulse alone
TSH, electrolytes, renal function; transthoracic echocardiogram for ventricular function and structural disease
Intermittent symptoms → ambulatory rhythm monitoring; assess reversible triggers

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable → **synchronized cardioversion**; do not delay for anticoagulation or TEE
Stable rate control: metoprolol or diltiazem; avoid diltiazem/verapamil with reduced EF
Decompensated HF: digoxin or amiodarone; preexcited AF: procainamide or cardioversion, no AV nodal blockers
Rhythm control for symptoms, early disease, or HF: cardioversion, selected antiarrhythmics, catheter ablation
★ Duration ≥48 hours/unknown: **3 weeks anticoagulation or TEE** before elective cardioversion; ≥4 weeks afterward

rows.label: Complications
items: **Top risk factor for cardioembolic stroke**, above age/hypertension; limb/gut emboli; tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy
Anticoagulant bleeding; rhythm drugs may cause proarrhythmia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Long-term anticoagulation: **CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 men/≥3 women**; consider one point lower
Apixaban/other DOAC preferred; mechanical valve or moderate/severe rheumatic mitral stenosis → warfarin
Weight reduction, BP/OSA treatment, limit alcohol
Aspirin no substitute for anticoagulation; adding aspirin to warfarin/DOAC → **more bleeding**, no added stroke protection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Atrial flutter: sawtooth atrial activity, often regular 2:1 conduction
Multifocal atrial tachycardia: ≥3 P-wave morphologies, isoelectric intervals

attachment-disorders.name: Attachment disorders
attachment-disorders.scope: Reactive attachment disorder, disinhibited social engagement disorder, pathogenic care and early severe neglect, emotional withdrawal, indiscriminate friendliness, trauma-informed therapy
attachment-disorders.core: Early severe neglect followed by abnormally withdrawn or indiscriminately social behavior toward adults.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ Pathogenic care: social neglect, repeated caregiver changes, institutional rearing with little individualized attention

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Developmental age ≥9 months; behavior inappropriate for developmental stage
Reactive attachment disorder: unexplained fear, sadness or irritability even during nonthreatening caregiver interactions
Disinhibited behavior may persist after adoption despite formation of selective attachments

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inconsistent or absent responsive caregiving disrupts selective attachment and regulation of distress

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Caregiver history plus observed interactions with familiar and unfamiliar adults
Verify severe insufficient care preceded behavior; assess development, trauma, and current safety
Disinhibited social engagement disorder: ≥2 characteristic behaviors; exclude isolated impulsivity

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Secure a **stable, responsive caregiver** and safe placement; report suspected ongoing maltreatment
Trauma-informed dyadic therapy, caregiver coaching, predictable routines
Treat comorbidities separately; avoid coercive holding or rebirthing therapies

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent peer and school difficulties; indiscriminate approach behavior raises exploitation risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early family support, consistent nurturing care, and minimizing placement disruptions

rows.label: Mimics
items: Autism: restricted interests, repetitive behaviors, pervasive social communication deficits
ADHD: generalized impulsivity across tasks, beyond approaches to unfamiliar adults

table.title: Two patterns
rows: Limited positive affect; onset before 5 years
Little checking back; readily leaves with stranger

attachment-disorders.evidence: Checked AACAP policy on coercive attachment interventions (2022); DSM-5-TR diagnostic teaching.

auricular-hematoma.name: Auricular hematoma
auricular-hematoma.scope: Blunt auricle trauma, subperichondrial hematoma, pinna fluctuance, needle aspiration, bolster pressure dressing, cauliflower ear deformity, empiric oral antibiotics
auricular-hematoma.core: Fluctuant pinna swelling after blunt trauma, requiring prompt evacuation to preserve cartilage.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Wrestling, boxing, rugby, other contact trauma; anticoagulation increases bleeding

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Tender swelling over cartilaginous pinna obscuring normal landmarks; lobule usually spared

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ Blood separates perichondrium from cartilage → disrupted nutrient supply and fibrocartilage overgrowth

rows.label: Dx
items: Clinical inspection and palpation; examine ear canal and tympanic membrane for associated trauma
Fever, marked erythema or purulence → consider secondary infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Small, very fresh collection → needle aspiration; larger, older, or recurrent → incision and drainage
★ Apply **bolster pressure dressing** for 5–7 days; recheck within 24–48 hours
Consider empiric oral antibiotics after drainage, e.g., ciprofloxacin when Pseudomonas coverage needed
Delayed or organized hematoma, recurrence or cartilage injury → ENT

rows.label: Complications
items: ★ Reaccumulation, cartilage necrosis, infection, permanent **cauliflower ear**

rows.label: Prevention
items: Protective headgear; avoid contact sports until healed

rows.label: Mimics
items: Perichondritis: hot erythematous cartilage, often after piercing
Auricular pseudocyst: painless, atraumatic swelling with serous fluid

auricular-hematoma.evidence: Established emergency care teaching; current antibiotic guidance not checked online.

benign-breast-conditions.name: Benign breast conditions
benign-breast-conditions.scope: Fibroadenoma, fibrocystic changes, intraductal papilloma, breast cyst, fat necrosis, galactocele, breast abscess
benign-breast-conditions.core: Breast symptoms require age-directed imaging and clinical–radiologic concordance; a benign-appearing examination alone cannot exclude malignancy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Reproductive hormonal cycling; milk stasis; breast trauma or prior surgery
Smoking predisposes to recurrent subareolar abscess
**Cracked, excoriated nipples** → main portal of entry for lactational mastitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Galactocele: cystic lactational/postlactational mass, no inflammation, varies with feeds; fat–fluid level on imaging
Mastitis: focal tender erythema, fever, no fluctuance; abscess adds **fluctuance**; often Staphylococcus aureus
★ Spontaneous unilateral **bloody single-duct discharge** → usually **papilloma**; exclude malignancy, persistent → surgical evaluation
Nonbloody discharge only on expression, normal exam → **physiologic**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hormone-responsive stromal/glandular tissue produces cyclic changes; duct obstruction causes retained secretions
Adipose injury causes inflammatory necrosis and calcification that can resemble cancer

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Palpable mass **<30 years → ultrasound**; ≥30 → diagnostic mammography with targeted ultrasound
Suspicious solid lesion or imaging–exam discordance → **core needle biopsy**
Simple cyst: anechoic, thin-walled, posterior enhancement; no solid component
Nonlactational abscess or persistent inflammation after antibiotics → exclude underlying carcinoma
Cyclic bilateral nodularity, no dominant mass → **reexamine after menses**, before imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Painful simple cyst → aspiration; nonbloody fluid + full collapse → benign; bloody fluid/residual mass → **biopsy**
Fibroadenoma → observe when concordant; excise if rapidly enlarging, large or symptomatic
Breast pain, no mass, young, normal exam → **reassurance**; fibrocystic pain → supportive bra, topical/oral NSAID
★ Mastitis → **dicloxacillin/cephalexin**, keep breastfeeding/pumping; abscess → add needle/incision drainage; MRSA → clindamycin
Tender lactating lump, no erythema/fever → **warm compresses**, keep nursing; persistent galactocele → aspiration

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent periductal abscess → fistula; incomplete drainage → persistent infection
Proliferative lesions with atypia increase future cancer risk; simple cysts do not

rows.label: Prevention
items: Effective breast emptying during lactation; smoking cessation for recurrent periductal disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cancer: irregular fixed mass, retraction or suspicious nodes
Phyllodes: rapidly enlarging fibroepithelial mass requiring excision

table.title: Common benign findings
rows: Early postpartum; bilateral tense tender breasts, low fever

benign-breast-conditions.evidence: Not checked online; established breast diagnostic principles.

benign-prostatic-hyperplasia.name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
benign-prostatic-hyperplasia.scope: Lower urinary tract symptoms, medical therapy, urinary retention and obstructive uropathy
benign-prostatic-hyperplasia.core: Aging man with hesitancy, weak stream, incomplete emptying, and nocturia from benign periurethral prostatic enlargement.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Increasing age, androgen exposure, family history, obesity/metabolic syndrome
Anticholinergics, opioids, and sympathomimetic decongestants can precipitate retention

rows.label: Clues
items: Storage symptoms: urgency, frequency; voiding symptoms: straining, intermittency, terminal dribbling
Smooth, symmetric enlarged prostate; size correlates imperfectly with symptom severity
★ **Painful inability to void** with palpable bladder → acute urinary retention
Renal dysfunction or bilateral hydronephrosis suggests high-pressure obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dihydrotestosterone-driven transition-zone hyperplasia + alpha-adrenergic smooth-muscle tone obstruct bladder outlet

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urinalysis**, symptom score, examination; review medications and neurologic disease
Postvoid residual if incomplete emptying suspected; creatinine/renal ultrasound for obstruction or renal impairment
PSA after shared decision-making if result changes management; elevation not specific for cancer

rows.label: Tx
items: Mild, nonbothersome → observation; reduce evening fluids, caffeine, alcohol; timed voiding
★ Acute retention → **urethral catheter**, then alpha-blocker and voiding trial; suprapubic drainage if catheterization fails
★ Refractory symptoms, retention, recurrent UTIs, stones, renal impairment → **TURP or other outlet procedure**
Monitor urine output/electrolytes after relief of prolonged obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Overflow incontinence, recurrent infection, bladder stones, postrenal AKI
Postobstructive diuresis; surgery → bleeding, retrograde ejaculation, urethral stricture

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid precipitating drugs; reassess progressive symptoms and residual volume
BPH does not transform into prostate cancer; continue independent cancer-risk discussion

rows.label: Mimics
items: Prostate cancer: hard asymmetric nodule
Prostatitis: tender prostate, fever; neurogenic bladder: neurologic disease, altered bladder sensation

table.title: Medication selection
rows: Large gland; reduce progression over months

bowel-obstruction.name: Bowel obstruction
bowel-obstruction.scope: Small bowel obstruction (adhesions, hernia), large bowel obstruction (volvulus, malignancy), paralytic ileus, NG decompression, surgical management
bowel-obstruction.core: Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distention, and obstipation suggest mechanical obstruction; constant pain or systemic toxicity raises concern for strangulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior abdominal surgery (**adhesions**, leading cause), incarcerated hernia, Crohn strictures → small-bowel obstruction
Colorectal malignancy, chronic constipation, institutionalization → large-bowel obstruction or sigmoid volvulus
Recent surgery, opioids, hypokalemia, severe systemic illness → ileus

rows.label: Clues
items: Early high-pitched sounds may become absent; proximal obstruction causes earlier vomiting, distal disease greater distention
★ **Peritonitis, fever, tachycardia, rising lactate**, or continuous severe pain → ischemia/perforation
Complete → **obstipation**, no flatus; partial may still pass stool/diarrhea, not excluding obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Luminal blockage → upstream dilation, third spacing; closed loop compromises venous then arterial supply
Adynamic ileus reflects impaired motility without an anatomic transition point

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast** defines transition point, cause, and ischemic signs
CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, lactate; normal lactate cannot exclude early ischemia
Radiograph may show dilated loops/air-fluid levels, no rectal gas; CT more definitive if diagnosis uncertain
★ Massive colonic distention + **coffee-bean (inverted-U) loop** on radiograph → sigmoid volvulus
Pregnancy: plain radiograph acceptable first (minimal fetal dose); MRI if unclear; do not delay

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, IV isotonic fluids, electrolyte correction**; NG decompression for significant vomiting/distention
★ Strangulation, perforation, closed loop, or incarcerated hernia → **urgent surgery** + ceftriaxone/metronidazole
Uncomplicated adhesive SBO → surgical observation, serial examination; water-soluble contrast helps predict resolution
Failure to improve during a short monitored trial, commonly up to 72 h → operation
Ileus → correct trigger, reduce opioids, mobilize; no operation solely for absent sounds

rows.label: Complications
items: Dehydration, AKI, hypokalemic alkalosis; bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis
Recurrent adhesions; short-bowel syndrome after extensive resection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early postoperative ambulation, opioid-sparing analgesia, electrolyte correction; elective repair of symptomatic hernias

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gastroenteritis: prominent diarrhea, no focal transition point
Mesenteric ischemia: pain out of proportion before peritoneal signs
Ileus: hypoactive/absent sounds, gas throughout bowel including rectum
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy: dysmotility, dilated loops without transition point

table.title: Large-bowel branches
rows: Sigmoidoscopic detorsion, rectal tube → same-admission resection

bowel-obstruction.evidence: Not checked online; established acute surgical management principles.

brain-death.name: Brain death
brain-death.scope: Prerequisites (normothermia, normal BP), clinical exam (coma, absent brainstem reflexes), apnea test, ancillary testing (cerebral blood flow studies)
brain-death.core: Permanent loss of all brain function, including brainstem function, constitutes death; a beating heart on ventilation does not negate the diagnosis.

rows.label: Principle
items: Known catastrophic irreversible brain injury; compatible neuroimaging; adequate observation period
No family consent needed; after declaration → stop ventilator, unless organ donation planned

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Prerequisites: **temperature ≥36°C**, adult SBP ≥100 and MAP ≥75 mm Hg
Exclude paralysis/metabolic confounders; sedatives: ≥5 half-lives, longer if impaired clearance
★ Examination: **coma**, no brain-mediated motor response; absent brainstem reflexes (table)

rows.label: Don't
items: Oculocephalic testing with possible cervical injury; use caloric testing after confirming ear integrity
Declare death with any brain-mediated response or spontaneous breath
Use ancillary testing to bypass hypothermia or high CNS-depressant levels

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Spinal reflex movements may persist without contradicting diagnosis
Incomplete examination or unsafe apnea test → radionuclide cerebral perfusion or catheter angiography
After temperature ≤35.5°C, wait ≥24 hours following rewarming to ≥36°C

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Apnea test: no breaths, **PaCO2 ≥60 and ≥20 above baseline**, pH <7.30
Preoxygenate; abort apnea testing for hypotension, hypoxemia or unstable arrhythmia
★ 2023 update: **EEG no longer accepted** as ancillary testing; pediatric requirements differ

brain-tumors.name: Brain tumors
brain-tumors.scope: Metastatic brain tumors, glioblastoma, meningioma, pediatric tumors (medulloblastoma), vestibular schwannoma
brain-tumors.core: Progressive focal deficits, new seizures or headache with raised intracranial pressure require brain imaging for a mass lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known lung, breast, melanoma, renal or colorectal malignancy → brain metastases
Prior cranial radiation; NF 2 predisposes to bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning headache, vomiting, papilledema; altered consciousness or pupillary asymmetry → impending herniation
Frontal → personality change; posterior fossa → ataxia; temporal (Meyer loop) → contralateral **superior quadrantanopia**
Pediatric posterior fossa mass can obstruct CSF flow and rapidly cause hydrocephalus
★ **Anosmia**, normal nasal exam, frontal release signs, papilledema → **subfrontal olfactory groove meningioma**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor disrupts local brain function and blood–brain barrier → vasogenic edema
Fixed cranial volume makes expanding tissue/CSF raise pressure and threaten brainstem perfusion
Astrocytoma grade, prognosis → **degree of histologic anaplasia**, not metastasis; extracranial spread rare

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Contrast MRI brain** best defines mass, edema and multiplicity; CT for unstable patients
Metastatic pattern → search primary with chest/abdominal imaging; tissue diagnosis when needed
★ Suspected mass with pressure signs → **avoid LP** until safe after imaging
Tinnitus, imbalance, facial weakness/numbness, altered taste (CN VII, V) → audiometry and MRI internal auditory canals

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic edema → **dexamethasone**; herniation → head elevation, hypertonic saline/mannitol, emergency neurosurgery
Seizure → levetiracetam; no routine antiseizure prophylaxis for every seizure-naive tumor patient
★ **Resection versus radiation** depends on lesion, symptoms, accessibility and systemic disease
Medulloblastoma → resection, chemotherapy and usually craniospinal radiation; avoid/delay radiation in very young children
Craniopharyngioma resection disrupts pituitary stalk → **lifelong pituitary hormone replacement**; watch central DI

rows.label: Complications
items: Obstructive hydrocephalus, herniation, hemorrhage, persistent neurologic deficits
Radiation injury, cognitive decline, steroid hyperglycemia and infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Abscess: infection context and central diffusion restriction
Primary CNS lymphoma: often periventricular; steroids can obscure biopsy
Stroke: abrupt maximal onset with vascular distribution; chronic subdural: prior head trauma
Ménière disease: episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss

table.title: Tumor distinctions
rows: Months of headache, deficits; necrotic, crosses corpus callosum
Woman; extra-axial, uniform enhancement, dural tail; parasagittal
Child; midline cerebellar mass; CSF drop metastases
CPA; insidious, high-frequency unilateral sensorineural hearing loss
Child; ataxia, nystagmus, head tilt, cranial neuropathies

brain-tumors.evidence: Not checked online; established neuro-oncology teaching.

breast-neoplasia.name: Breast neoplasia
breast-neoplasia.scope: Ductal carcinoma in situ, invasive ductal and lobular carcinoma, receptor status (ER, PR, HER2), metastatic disease (bone, visceral), surgical management, endocrine and chemotherapy
breast-neoplasia.core: A suspicious breast lesion requires core biopsy, assessment of invasion and ER/PR/HER2 status to guide local and systemic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Increasing age, BRCA-related syndromes, close-relative family history (distant relative adds little), prior chest irradiation
**Combined estrogen-progestin therapy**, prolonged estrogen, postmenopausal obesity, alcohol; atypical proliferative lesions

rows.label: Clues
items: Painless hard irregular mass, skin/nipple retraction, unilateral bloody discharge or axillary node
★ Peau d’orange, diffuse erythema and edema → **inflammatory breast cancer**, even without discrete mass
Persistent unilateral eczematous nipple lesion → Paget disease; **full-thickness biopsy**, investigate underlying carcinoma

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Invasion through basement membrane enables lymphatic/hematogenous metastasis
ER/PR signaling and HER2 amplification create actionable tumor drivers; triple-negative tumors lack these targets

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Diagnostic mammography + targeted ultrasound** → core biopsy of suspicious lesion; pregnancy → **ultrasound first**
Pathology: invasion, grade, **ER/PR/HER2**; assess regional nodes clinically and with targeted imaging
Clinically node-negative invasive disease, including microinvasion ≤1 mm → sentinel node biopsy during definitive surgery
Distant staging scans for advanced disease or suspicious symptoms; not every small asymptomatic cancer
Axillary node adenocarcinoma, normal mammogram → occult breast primary; breast MRI

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early: lumpectomy + radiation or mastectomy; **positive margins → reexcision** before adjuvant therapy
ER-positive → tamoxifen or postmenopausal aromatase inhibitor; chemotherapy based on stage/biology
★ HER2-positive → **trastuzumab-based** treatment, monitor LVEF; triple-negative → chemotherapy ± pembrolizumab if higher-risk
Locally advanced → neoadjuvant treatment, then surgery/radiation; large residual + palpable nodes → **mastectomy + axillary dissection**
Bone metastases → **zoledronate/denosumab**; systemic treatment by receptors, chemotherapy for visceral crisis

rows.label: Complications
items: Metastases to bone (often **mixed lytic–blastic**), lung, liver, brain; surgery/radiation → lymphedema
Tamoxifen → VTE/endometrial cancer; aromatase inhibitors → bone loss; trastuzumab → cardiomyopathy
Prior cancer + severe hypercalcemia, lytic lesions → recurrence; thiazide/calcium supplements cause only mild elevation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Age/risk-based screening, genetic counseling for suggestive pedigree; selected high-risk patients → chemoprevention
BRCA-related very high risk → discuss risk-reducing surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mastitis: lactation-associated tenderness/fever, improves with antibiotics
Fat necrosis: trauma/surgery history; biopsy if discordant imaging

table.title: Histologic distinctions
rows: Bilateral risk marker; discohesive lobular cells
Surveillance/risk reduction if concordant; later cancer usually ductal

breast-neoplasia.evidence: Not checked online; established breast-oncology management principles.

bronchiectasis.name: Bronchiectasis
bronchiectasis.scope: Cystic fibrosis, post-infectious, high-resolution CT, airway clearance, pseudomonas colonization, acute exacerbation
bronchiectasis.core: Chronic productive cough with recurrent respiratory infections and permanently dilated bronchi on high-resolution CT.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Cystic fibrosis, prior severe pneumonia/TB, primary ciliary dyskinesia, aspiration, immunodeficiency
ABPA, rheumatoid arthritis, obstructing endobronchial lesion; some cases remain idiopathic

rows.label: Clues
items: Copious purulent sputum, coarse crackles, recurrent focal infections, hemoptysis, sometimes clubbing
Exacerbation: increased sputum volume/purulence, cough, dyspnea, fatigue; hypoxemia or sepsis → severe disease
Early lifelong infections, sinusitis, infertility, or situs inversus suggest impaired ciliary clearance
Child: chronic cough refractory to bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics + persistent focal collapse/consolidation → localized bronchiectasis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impaired mucus clearance → persistent infection and neutrophilic inflammation → irreversible airway wall destruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **High-resolution chest CT**: signet-ring bronchi, absent tapering, airways visible near pleura, cystic spaces ± air-fluid levels
Sputum bacterial and mycobacterial cultures; spirometry measures associated airflow limitation
Quantitative immunoglobulins; total IgE/Aspergillus testing for ABPA; sweat chloride if CF suspected
Localized disease → bronchoscopy for tumor/foreign body; diffuse disease → investigate systemic cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Daily **airway clearance**, exercise; bronchodilator for obstruction; no routine inhaled steroids or non-CF dornase alfa
★ Exacerbation → sputum culture then antibiotics guided by prior isolates; often **14 days**
Pseudomonas susceptible → ciprofloxacin; severe infection → IV cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam
★ ≥2 yearly or ≥1 severe exacerbation → azithromycin after NTM exclusion; chronic Pseudomonas → inhaled tobramycin
Massive hemoptysis → airway protection and bronchial artery embolization; focal refractory disease → resection evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic Pseudomonas colonization, resistant infection, respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension
Antibiotic toxicity/resistance; macrolides can cause QT prolongation and hearing impairment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, influenza/pneumococcal vaccination, aspiration management, treatment of underlying immunodeficiency
New Pseudomonas isolation → specialist eradication regimen, often ciprofloxacin followed by inhaled antibiotic

rows.label: Mimics
items: Chronic bronchitis: smoking-related sputum without characteristic bronchial dilation
Lung abscess: solitary cavity with air-fluid level; no lifelong productive cough
Pulmonary TB: constitutional illness and compatible imaging; mycobacterial testing confirms

bronchiolitis.name: Bronchiolitis
bronchiolitis.scope: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), infant wheezing, respiratory distress, hypoxemia, supplemental oxygen, nasal suctioning, palivizumab prophylaxis indications
bronchiolitis.core: Infant with a viral prodrome followed by a first episode of diffuse wheezing or crackles: supportive care is the main treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age <2 years, winter exposure, daycare; RSV commonest cause
Severe disease: age <12 weeks, prematurity, chronic lung disease, significant congenital heart disease, immunodeficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachypnea, retractions, nasal flaring, reduced intake; examination may fluctuate after suctioning
★ Apnea, exhaustion, cyanosis, dehydration → admission and escalation
Very young infants may present with apnea without prominent lower-airway findings

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Viral injury → small-airway edema, mucus plugging, air trapping, patchy atelectasis
Ventilation–perfusion mismatch causes hypoxemia; tiny infant airways increase obstruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; no routine chest radiograph, viral testing, CBC, or blood cultures
Assess work of breathing, hydration, and oxygenation; investigate focal findings or atypical course
Radiographic atelectasis can mimic pneumonia and drive unnecessary antibiotics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Gentle **nasal suctioning** + small frequent feeds; NG/IV fluids if intake inadequate
★ Persistent SpO2 <90% → oxygen; worsening distress → high-flow support, CPAP/intubation if failing
No routine albuterol, epinephrine, corticosteroids, antibiotics, or chest physiotherapy
Antibiotics only for documented/suspected bacterial coinfection; avoid deep repetitive suctioning

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure, apnea, dehydration; later recurrent wheezing association
Cough may persist for weeks despite improving respiratory effort

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Hand hygiene, smoke avoidance; maternal RSV vaccine or infant antibody protection
Age <8 months: nirsevimab/clesrovimab if maternal vaccination absent/unknown or birth <14 days afterward
Age 8–19 months, second season: nirsevimab for selected high-risk children, including severe immunocompromise
Palivizumab: historical board option; US availability ended 2025; current long-acting antibodies replace it

rows.label: Mimics
items: Asthma: recurrent episodes, older child, atopic history
Foreign body: abrupt onset, unilateral wheeze
Bacterial pneumonia: focal consolidation, toxic appearance

carcinoid-syndrome.name: Carcinoid syndrome
carcinoid-syndrome.scope: Neuroendocrine tumors (midgut, bronchial), episodic cutaneous flushing, secretory diarrhea, tricuspid and pulmonary valvular disease, 24-hour urine 5-HIAA, octreotide therapy, surgical resection
carcinoid-syndrome.core: Episodic flushing and secretory diarrhea in a patient with a neuroendocrine tumor, often with liver metastases.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Midgut NET, especially ileal; bronchial NET with systemic venous drainage

rows.label: Clues
items: Watery stools persist during fasting; episodic wheezing
★ Right-sided valve disease: **tricuspid regurgitation** and pulmonic stenosis; edema, JVD
Left-sided valve disease possible with bronchial NET or right-to-left intracardiac shunt
Carcinoid crisis: abrupt hypotension or hypertension, bronchospasm and hemodynamic instability

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hepatic metabolism normally clears portal vasoactive products; hepatic metastases or systemic drainage bypass first pass
Serotonin drives diarrhea and endocardial fibrosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **24-hour urine 5-HIAA**; avoid serotonin-rich foods and interfering drugs before collection
CT/MRI and somatostatin receptor PET for localization and staging; tissue grading guides tumor therapy
NT-proBNP >260 pg/mL or cardiac signs → echocardiogram

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Octreotide** or lanreotide for hormonal symptoms and tumor control
Resect localized disease; selected metastatic cases → hepatic debulking or liver-directed therapy
Refractory diarrhea despite somatostatin analog → add telotristat
★ Carcinoid crisis → IV octreotide, fluids, vasopressors

rows.label: Complications
items: Right heart failure; mesenteric fibrosis → obstruction or ischemia
Tryptophan diversion → niacin deficiency and pellagra

rows.label: Prevention
items: Periprocedural planning for crisis risk during anesthesia or tumor manipulation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pheochromocytoma: episodic hypertension, headache, diaphoresis
VIPoma: profound watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria

carcinoid-syndrome.evidence: Checked ENETS guidance on carcinoid syndrome and carcinoid heart disease (2022).

celiac-disease.name: Celiac disease
celiac-disease.scope: Gluten-sensitive enteropathy, malabsorption, iron deficiency anemia, dermatitis herpetiformis, IgA anti-tTG, small bowel villous atrophy, gluten-free diet
celiac-disease.core: Gluten-triggered autoimmune small-bowel injury causing malabsorption or unexplained iron deficiency, sometimes with intensely pruritic extensor-surface dermatitis herpetiformis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: First-degree relative, type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, selective IgA deficiency
HLA-DQ2/DQ8 susceptibility; positive genotype common and not diagnostic

rows.label: Clues
items: Chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, bloating, weight loss; constipation or minimal GI symptoms possible
Iron deficiency refractory to oral replacement, aphthous ulcers, low bone density
Children: poor growth/delayed puberty; severe disease: hypoalbuminemia, edema, vitamin deficiencies

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tissue transglutaminase modifies gliadin → T-cell response damages proximal intestinal mucosa
Impaired absorption → iron/folate deficiency; cutaneous granular IgA deposition causes rash
Fat malabsorption → **vitamin D deficiency** → low calcium + low phosphate; hypoparathyroidism instead raises phosphate

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ While **eating gluten → IgA anti-tTG (or anti-endomysial) + total IgA**; gluten restriction causes false negatives
★ IgA deficiency → **IgG anti-tTG or deamidated gliadin peptide antibodies**
★ Adults: positive serology or high suspicion → **EGD with multiple duodenal biopsies**, even if mucosa normal
