Biopsy: villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytes; high suspicion overrides negative serology

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Lifelong gluten-free diet**: avoid wheat, barley, rye; dietitian, cross-contamination counseling
Pure uncontaminated oats usually tolerated; replace iron, folate, calcium, vitamin D and other measured deficiencies
Dermatitis herpetiformis: dapsone for rapid relief after G6PD testing; diet treats underlying intestinal injury
Persistent symptoms → assess gluten exposure, alternative diagnoses; refractory disease → specialist before immunosuppression

rows.label: Complications
items: Osteoporosis, infertility; untreated disease → enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma, small-bowel adenocarcinoma
Dapsone → hemolysis/methemoglobinemia; restrictive diet → nutritional imbalance

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Follow **symptoms, nutritional labs, anti-tTG trend**; persistent elevation suggests gluten exposure
Bone-density assessment in adults with risk/malabsorption; test symptomatic first-degree relatives
No proven primary prevention; do not start gluten exclusion before diagnostic testing

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBS: no objective malabsorption, anemia, or inflammatory injury
Giardiasis: contaminated water exposure, stool antigen/PCR positive
Pancreatic insufficiency: low fecal elastase, **normal D-xylose absorption** (low in mucosal disease)

cervicitis-pid.name: Cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease
cervicitis-pid.core: Sexually active patient with mucopurulent discharge or postcoital bleeding; ascending infection adds pelvic pain, sometimes an adnexal abscess.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age <25 (adolescent cervical ectopy → vulnerable columnar epithelium), new/multiple partners, inconsistent condoms, prior STI
IUD-associated PID risk concentrated within first 3 weeks after insertion

rows.label: Clues
items: Cervical friability, easily induced endocervical bleeding; infection sometimes asymptomatic
Dyspareunia, fever; severe unilateral pain/adnexal mass → **tubo-ovarian abscess**
Peritonitis, shock → rupture; RUQ pain → Fitz-Hugh–Curtis perihepatitis
Persistent dysuria, sterile pyuria, negative culture → chlamydial urethritis, not UTI

rows.label: Pathophys
items: GC/CT ascend cervix → endometrium/tubes; PID often polymicrobial, including anaerobes
Chlamydial tubal damage: **host immune response** → scarring, hydrosalpinx

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pregnancy test** first; vaginal/cervical or urine **GC/CT NAAT**; HIV/syphilis testing
★ Pelvic pain + **cervical motion, uterine, OR adnexal tenderness** → presumptive PID; no confirmation delay
Negative cervical NAAT does not exclude upper-tract infection; normal discharge/no vaginal leukocytes argues against PID
**Transvaginal US** for abscess or diagnostic uncertainty; routine laparoscopy unnecessary

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Cervicitis: empiric GC/CT coverage IF high risk/unreliable follow-up; otherwise await NAAT
★ Admit IF **pregnant, abscess, severe illness**, oral intolerance, uncertain surgical diagnosis, or failure by 72 h
Abscess rupture → emergency surgery; persistent abscess after 48–72 h antibiotics → drainage
Pregnant chlamydia → **azithromycin**, avoid doxycycline; retain IUD initially, reassess if no improvement

rows.label: Complications
items: Tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain; abscess → sepsis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Treat partners from prior **60 days**; abstain until courses completed, partners treated, symptoms resolved
Retest GC/CT at 3 months; pregnant chlamydia → test of cure at 4 weeks
Annual GC/CT screening: sexually active women <25, older women with risks; condoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ectopic pregnancy: positive hCG, no confirmed intrauterine pregnancy
Ovarian torsion: abrupt unilateral pain, vomiting; Doppler flow may persist
Appendicitis: migrating RLQ pain, CT appendiceal inflammation

table.title: Antibiotic branches
rows: Ceftriaxone; add CT regimen unless excluded
Oral drugs 14 days; ceftriaxone once IM outpatient

child-growth-and-development.name: Child growth and development
child-growth-and-development.scope: Normal growth velocity, weight doubling and tripling milestones, WHO/CDC growth chart interpretation, developmental surveillance, normal toddler behavioral variants (head banging, temper tantrums)
child-growth-and-development.core: Interpret serial growth and developmental progress against age, family pattern, and corrected gestational age; a trajectory matters more than one percentile.

rows.label: Definition
items: Weight doubles by 4–6 months, triples by 12 months, quadruples near 24 months
Length increases about 25 cm during year 1; prepubertal height velocity about 5–6 cm/year
★ **WHO charts before 2 years; CDC charts from 2 years** in US practice

rows.label: Interpret
items: Nutrition failure: weight falls first; endocrine disease: height slows with preserved/increased weight
★ Falling **2 major percentile channels**, well child → **diet diary, calorie counts** before labs
Correct prematurity through about 2 years; track infant head circumference

rows.label: Use when
items: Developmental surveillance every visit; standardized general screens at 9, 18, and 30 months
★ **Regression/missed milestones → early intervention**; language delay → **audiometry** before speech testing
BMI-for-age from 2 years; weight-for-length younger; consider parental heights and pubertal timing

rows.label: Compare
items: Tantrums, picky eating, bedtime separation distress → reassure, routines, calm limits; no sedatives
Head banging at sleep onset or frustration, normal development → self-soothing; assess injuries
Preschool restlessness, good function → no stimulants; overwhelmed parent → **parenting classes**

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **One percentile cannot diagnose disease**; stable tracking + normal exam → reassure
Persistent skill loss needs evaluation; never wait for school failure
Short parents, normal bone age → familial; average parents, delayed puberty → **constitutional delay**

rows.label: Adolescence
items: ★ Moodiness, privacy, family detachment, rule-questioning, late bedtimes, good function → reassure, educate parents
Parental-pressure conflict, occasional experimentation, no impairment → not ODD, substance use disorder
Weight worry, stable percentile, normal BMI, regular menses → normal; not eating disorder

table.title: Normal by age
rows: Holds head up; not yet reaching
Sits unsupported; bangs blocks, self-feeds finger foods
Walks; scribbles; non-walker at 14 months normal
Balances on one foot; copies circle
Same-sex parent preference; involve other parent otherwise

child-growth-and-development.evidence: Checked screening ages 2026-10-30: [AAP surveillance/screening](https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/developmental-surveillance-and-screening-patient-care/); growth facts established pediatric teaching.

chlamydia-infection.name: Chlamydia infection
chlamydia-infection.scope: Chlamydia trachomatis, nongonococcal urethritis, cervicitis, lymphogranuloma venereum, neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia, NAAT screening and diagnosis, doxycycline and azithromycin
chlamydia-infection.core: Often silent sexually transmitted intracellular infection causing urethritis or cervicitis; untreated infection threatens fertility and can infect newborns during delivery.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age <25 years, new/multiple partners, inconsistent condom use, infected partner; perinatal exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: Dysuria, scant discharge, sterile pyuria; friable cervix, mucopurulent discharge, postcoital/intermenstrual bleeding
★ Neonatal conjunctivitis at **5–12 days**; afebrile staccato pneumonia at **1–3 months**
LGV: transient painless genital ulcer → tender inguinal nodes/buboes or invasive proctocolitis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: C. trachomatis: obligate intracellular bacterium; D–K serovars cause genital/perinatal infection, L1–L3 cause LGV

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **NAAT**: vaginal swab preferred in women; first-catch urine in men; rectal swab after exposure
Test for gonorrhea, HIV, syphilis; fever, pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness → evaluate for PID
Infant conjunctival testing requires epithelial cells; nasopharyngeal testing for pneumonia
Sexually active MSM: annual site-specific screening; every 3–6 months with persistent high risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated infection → **doxycycline for 7 days**; LGV → 21 days
★ Pregnancy → **azithromycin**, single dose; alternative when adherence doubtful, less reliable for rectal infection
Neonatal disease → oral erythromycin for 14 days; azithromycin alternative; topical treatment alone inadequate
Gonorrhea suspected or detected → add ceftriaxone; PID requires broader multidrug coverage

rows.label: Complications
items: PID → tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain; epididymitis, reactive arthritis
LGV → rectal strictures/fistulas; infant macrolides → hypertrophic pyloric stenosis risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Treat partners from preceding **60 days**; expedited partner treatment where legal
Abstain until 7-day course completed or 7 days after single dose, and partners treated
★ **Annual NAAT**: sexually active women <25 despite condoms; older if risk; pregnancy entry; Pap from 21
Retest at 3 months; pregnancy test-of-cure at 4 weeks; neonatal eye ointment does not prevent chlamydia

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gonorrhea: copious purulent discharge, Gram-stain intracellular diplococci; **neutrophils alone** → nongonococcal urethritis, usually chlamydia
M. genitalium: persistent nongonococcal urethritis after doxycycline; separate NAAT
HSV: painful ulcers and external dysuria rather than isolated cervical discharge
Cystitis: suprapubic tenderness, bacteriuria; urethritis → **distal anterior vaginal wall tenderness**, sterile pyuria

chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia.name: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia.scope: Asymptomatic lymphocytosis, smudge cells, flow cytometry (CD5/CD19/CD20/CD23), Rai/Binet staging, hypogammaglobulinemia, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Richter transformation
chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia.core: An older adult with persistent clonal mature B-cell lymphocytosis may have indolent CLL requiring observation rather than immediate treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, male sex, family history; frequently discovered incidentally on CBC

rows.label: Clues
items: Painless lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly; smear with small mature lymphocytes and **smudge cells**
Recurrent sinopulmonary infection suggests hypogammaglobulinemia
★ Rapid asymmetric node growth, fever, weight loss and ↑LDH → **Richter transformation**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Accumulation of dysfunctional clonal B lymphocytes in blood, marrow and lymphoid tissue
Immune dysregulation causes antibody deficiency and autoimmune cytopenias

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Flow cytometry**: clonal B cells coexpress **CD5/CD19/CD23**, weak CD20 and surface immunoglobulin
Clonal B-cell count **≥5000/µL for ≥3 months** supports CLL; lower count without disease → MBL
Smudge cells alone not diagnostic; nodal disease with lower circulating count → SLL
CBC, examination, hemolysis studies/DAT for anemia; marrow biopsy not routinely needed for diagnosis
Before treatment: assess TP53/del(17p), IGHV and TLS risk; suspected transformation → node biopsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Asymptomatic early disease → **watchful waiting** with clinical/CBC follow-up
Progressive marrow failure, bulky symptomatic disease, B symptoms or refractory autoimmune cytopenias → treatment
**Acalabrutinib/zanubrutinib** or venetoclax + obinutuzumab; regimen chosen by genetics/comorbidity
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia → glucocorticoids; severe recurrent infections with low IgG → selected IVIG
Venetoclax → gradual escalation with tumor-lysis prevention and monitoring

rows.label: Complications
items: Bacterial infections, warm autoimmune hemolysis, immune thrombocytopenia, second cancers
BTK inhibitors → bleeding/atrial arrhythmia; anti-CD20 drugs → HBV reactivation

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Vaccinate before immunosuppression; avoid live vaccines during significant immunocompromise
Screen HBV before anti-CD20 treatment; skin surveillance and routine cancer screening

rows.label: Mimics
items: Reactive lymphocytosis: transient, polyclonal cells
Mantle cell lymphoma: CD5-positive but usually CD23-negative, cyclin D1-positive

clostridioides-difficile-infection.name: Clostridioides difficile infection
clostridioides-difficile-infection.scope: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea, toxic megacolon, pseudomembranous colitis, NAAT vs EIA stool toxin testing, oral fidaxomicin, oral vancomycin, fulminant colitis
clostridioides-difficile-infection.core: Recent antibiotics or healthcare exposure followed by watery diarrhea suggests toxin-mediated colitis; ileus can conceal fulminant disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins, penicillins, even perioperative; older age, hospitalization, immunosuppression
Prior infection and unnecessary acid suppression increase susceptibility or recurrence

rows.label: Clues
items: Onset during or weeks after antibiotics; fecal leukocytes, occasionally blood/mucus; pseudomembranes on endoscopy
Abdominal cramps, fever, leukocytosis; severe disease may cause AKI and hypoalbuminemia
★ **Hypotension, ileus, or megacolon** defines fulminant infection; diarrhea may disappear

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fecal-oral **ingested spores**; antibiotic disruption of colonic microbiota permits toxigenic bacilli to proliferate
Exotoxins A and B damage colonic epithelium → inflammation and pseudomembranes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Test **unformed stool** with ≥3 unexplained stools/24 hours; exclude laxative effect
NAAT detects toxigenic genes, not active toxin; positive results can represent colonization
Toxin EIA is less sensitive; multistep GDH/NAAT plus toxin improves clinical specificity
No test of cure; abdominal imaging for distention, toxicity, or suspected perforation

rows.label: Tx
items: Stop inciting antibiotic when possible; replace fluids/electrolytes, avoid antimotility drugs in severe colitis
★ Initial nonfulminant infection: **oral fidaxomicin** preferred; oral vancomycin acceptable, usually 10 days
★ Fulminant: **high-dose oral/NG vancomycin + IV metronidazole**; add rectal vancomycin with ileus
Shock, perforation, worsening organ failure → urgent surgical consultation
Recurrence: fidaxomicin or tapered/pulsed vancomycin; multiple recurrences → screened microbiota-based treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Toxic megacolon, perforation, sepsis, recurrent infection
Severe classification: WBC >15,000/µL or creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL; different from fulminant criteria

rows.label: Prevention
items: Contact precautions, gloves/gown, soap-and-water handwashing, sporicidal surface cleaning
Antibiotic stewardship; no screening/treatment of asymptomatic carriers

rows.label: Mimics
items: Laxative-associated diarrhea: medication timing, no inflammatory syndrome
IBD flare: chronic relapsing course; test for coinfection before escalating immunosuppression
Shigella/Salmonella: dysentery after food or travel exposure, no recent antibiotic

colorectal-carcinoma.name: Colorectal carcinoma
colorectal-carcinoma.scope: Colon adenocarcinoma, rectal cancer, staging, surgical resection (hemicolectomy), liver metastases, chemotherapy
colorectal-carcinoma.core: Occult blood loss, altered bowel habits, or obstruction warrants colon evaluation; cancer stage determines local and systemic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, adenomas, Lynch/FAP, longstanding colitis, family history; smoking, obesity, processed meat

rows.label: Clues
items: Right-sided lesions → iron-deficiency anemia, fatigue, occult bleeding
Left-sided lesions → constipation, narrowed stools, obstruction; rectal lesions → tenesmus/hematochezia
Weight loss, palpable mass; hepatomegaly or elevated ALP suggests hepatic spread
Bladder invasion → colovesical fistula: fecaluria, mixed fecal flora in urine

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Adenoma–carcinoma sequence involves APC, KRAS, p53; mismatch-repair failure drives microsatellite instability
Portal drainage favors liver metastases; distal rectal tumors may spread directly to lungs

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Colonoscopy with biopsy**; evaluate entire colon for synchronous tumors
★ Confirmed cancer → **CT chest/abdomen/pelvis**, baseline CEA, tumor mismatch-repair/MSI testing
Rectal cancer → pelvic MRI for local staging; CEA cannot diagnose or screen
Obstruction/perforation → urgent contrast CT and surgical assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Resectable colon cancer → **segmental colectomy with lymphadenectomy**; selected liver metastases → resection
Stage III → adjuvant FOLFOX/CAPOX; selected high-risk stage II → individualized chemotherapy
Locally advanced rectal cancer → neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy/chemoradiation, then total mesorectal excision
Unresectable metastases, nonobstructing primary → **chemotherapy**, no primary resection; MSI-high → checkpoint inhibitor
Perforation or unstable obstruction → urgent operation; selected stable obstruction → stent or diversion

rows.label: Complications
items: Bleeding, perforation, malignant obstruction; venous thrombosis; oxaliplatin neuropathy
Postoperative anastomotic leak; pelvic treatment → urinary/sexual dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Average-risk screening **45–75 years**; earlier colonoscopy for strong family history/hereditary syndromes
Postresection colonoscopy, CEA and stage-based CT surveillance; remove premalignant polyps

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hemorrhoids: outlet bleeding without explanatory anemia; do not dismiss alarm features
IBD: chronic inflammatory diarrhea; diverticulitis: acute focal pain and fever

colorectal-carcinoma.evidence: Screening checked 2026-10-30: [USPSTF colorectal screening](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/colorectal-cancer-screening); treatment: established oncology teaching.

table.title: TNM essentials
rows: Extension through muscle; no regional nodal spread

colorectal-polyps-and-polyposis-syndrome.name: Colorectal polyps and polyposis syndromes
colorectal-polyps-and-polyposis-syndrome.scope: Adenomatous polyps, serrated polyps, familial adenomatous polyposis, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, juvenile polyposis
colorectal-polyps-and-polyposis-syndrome.core: Colorectal polyps differ in malignant potential; numerous lesions or characteristic extraintestinal findings suggest an inherited cancer syndrome.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, family history, obesity, smoking; pathogenic germline variants in hereditary polyposis

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually incidental; occult bleeding or iron-deficiency anemia; large distal polyps may prolapse
Childhood painless rectal bleeding → solitary juvenile polyp; recurrent pain → hamartoma-associated intussusception
★ **Mucocutaneous lip pigmentation** with hamartomatous polyps → Peutz-Jeghers
Serrated crypts: proximal sessile lesions premalignant, unlike typical small distal hyperplastic polyps

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Conventional adenomas progress through dysplasia; sessile serrated lesions follow a distinct molecular pathway
Hamartomas contain disorganized native tissue; syndromic forms carry cancer risk despite benign-appearing histology

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Colonoscopy with complete polypectomy and histology** defines type and surveillance
Advanced adenoma: ≥10 mm, villous component, or high-grade dysplasia
Numerous adenomas, young age, syndromic features → genetic counseling/testing
≥5 juvenile colorectal polyps, other GI juvenile polyps, or family history → juvenile polyposis evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Remove adenomatous/serrated lesions; incomplete or unresectable lesion → advanced endoscopy or surgery
FAP → **prophylactic colectomy** when burden/dysplasia cannot be controlled; continue retained-rectum surveillance
Hamartomatous syndromes → endoscopic removal of large/symptomatic polyps; surgery for obstruction or uncontrolled burden

rows.label: Complications
items: Colorectal cancer; postpolypectomy bleeding/perforation; intussusception and anemia in hamartomatous disease
FAP → duodenal cancer, desmoid tumors; Peutz-Jeghers → pancreatic, breast and gynecologic cancers

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Family cascade testing; syndrome-specific colon and upper-GI surveillance
Low-risk 1–2 small tubular adenomas → repeat colonoscopy 7–10 years after high-quality examination
Advanced adenoma → generally 3 years; shorten for large piecemeal resection or numerous lesions

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sporadic hyperplastic polyp: small rectosigmoid lesion, usually negligible cancer risk
Lynch syndrome: few polyps, mismatch-repair defect, colorectal/endometrial cancers

colorectal-polyps-and-polyposis-syndrome.evidence: Surveillance checked 2026-10-30: [US Multi-Society Task Force, 2020](https://www.asge.org/home/resources/publications/guidelines/recommendations-for-follow-up-after-colonoscopy-and-polypectomy-a-consensus-update-by-the-us-multi-society-task-force-on-colorectal-cancer); syndromes: established teaching.

compartment-syndrome.name: Compartment syndrome
compartment-syndrome.scope: Acute compartment syndrome, 6 Ps, pain with passive stretch, intracompartmental pressure measurement, emergent fasciotomy
compartment-syndrome.core: Rapidly increasing pressure inside a closed fascial space compromises microvascular perfusion; urgent decompression prevents irreversible muscle and nerve death.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Tibial/forearm fractures, crush injury, reperfusion after arterial occlusion, electrical burns
Tight casts or dressings, bleeding disorders, anticoagulation; prolonged immobilization with limb compression

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Early **pain out of proportion**, escalating analgesic requirement, tense swollen compartment
★ **Pain with passive stretch** of involved muscles; paresthesia follows
Six Ps: pain, paresthesia, pallor, paralysis, pulselessness, poikilothermia; latter findings usually late
★ **Normal pulses do not exclude**; capillary flow fails before large-artery flow

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Interstitial pressure rises → venous outflow obstruction → worsening edema and tissue ischemia
Ischemic cell swelling amplifies pressure; injury progresses despite initially preserved systemic perfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Convincing examination → **clinical diagnosis**; do not wait for imaging or pressure measurement
Unreliable examination or uncertainty → measure pressure in all suspected compartments
Diastolic BP minus compartment pressure **≤30 mm Hg** supports diagnosis; interpret with examination/trend
Serial neurovascular assessments after high-risk injury; CK and creatinine assess muscle breakdown, not exclusion

rows.label: Tx
items: Remove restrictive casts/dressings; keep limb **at heart level**, correct hypotension
★ **Emergent fasciotomy** of all involved compartments; orthopedic/vascular consultation immediately
IV fluids and electrolyte monitoring with rhabdomyolysis; debride nonviable tissue during staged care
Do not elevate high above heart or delay for restoration of distal pulse

rows.label: Complications
items: Volkmann ischemic contracture, permanent sensory/motor loss, limb loss
Rhabdomyolysis → hyperkalemia, myoglobinuric AKI; infection after tissue necrosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid constrictive dressings; reassess swelling after fracture reduction and revascularization
Prophylactic fasciotomy in selected prolonged-ischemia revascularization or severe crush injuries

rows.label: Mimics
items: Acute arterial occlusion: early pulse loss, cold pale limb; may coexist
DVT: swelling without marked passive-stretch pain or tense fascial compartment
Cellulitis: superficial erythema/warmth rather than pressure-related neuromuscular findings

compartment-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established surgical emergency teaching.

congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia.name: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia.core: Newborn salt loss or atypical genitalia demands adrenal evaluation; hypertension with abnormal puberty suggests a different steroid-synthesis block.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autosomal recessive inheritance; affected sibling, consanguinity
Classic disease presents neonatally; partial enzyme deficiency may present with adolescent androgen excess

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Neonatal vomiting, weight loss, dehydration, **shock**, ↓Na, ↓glucose → salt-wasting adrenal crisis
46,XX virilization with internal female organs; 46,XY infants may lack obvious external warning signs
Nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency: premature pubarche, hirsutism, acne or irregular menses

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Low cortisol removes feedback → ↑ACTH and adrenal hyperplasia
Steroid precursors accumulate upstream; androgen and mineralocorticoid effects depend on enzyme block

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **17-hydroxyprogesterone** screens for 21-hydroxylase deficiency; elevated values → confirmatory steroid testing
Borderline nonclassic disease → ACTH-stimulated 17-OHP; electrolytes, renin, cortisol and androgens guide subtype
Ambiguous genitalia → karyotype, pelvic ultrasound, endocrine consultation; avoid premature sex assignment
Newborn screen may miss milder disease; clinical instability overrides screening results

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Crisis → **IV hydrocortisone**, isotonic saline, dextrose; treat severe hyperkalemia
Glucocorticoid replacement suppresses ACTH; salt-wasting forms → fludrocortisone plus infant salt supplementation
11β/17α-associated hypertension → glucocorticoids; add antihypertensives for persistent elevation
Genital differences → multidisciplinary counseling; timing of surgery requires informed shared decisions

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated crisis → death; androgen excess → precocious pseudopuberty, advanced bone age, short adult height
Excess replacement → growth suppression, obesity, osteoporosis; inadequate replacement → infertility/adrenal rest tumors

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Newborn screening, genetic counseling; emergency steroid kit, medical alert, illness/surgery stress dosing

rows.label: Mimics
items: Androgen insensitivity: 46,XY, testes, absent uterus, normal adrenal steroids
Pyloric stenosis: vomiting with hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis rather than salt-wasting hyperkalemia

congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

congenital-heart-disease.name: Congenital heart disease
congenital-heart-disease.scope: Cyanotic heart disease (5 Ts: Tetralogy of Fallot, TGA, truncus, tricuspid atresia, TAPVR), acyanotic heart disease (VSD, ASD, PDA, coarctation of aorta), hyperoxia test, prostaglandin E1
congenital-heart-disease.core: Neonatal cyanosis or shock as the ductus closes demands urgent assessment for duct-dependent congenital heart disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Maternal diabetes, congenital rubella, family history; Down syndrome → AV septal defects
Prematurity → PDA; Turner syndrome → coarctation

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor feeding, diaphoresis, tachypnea, hepatomegaly → infant heart failure
VSD: harsh holosystolic lower-left sternal murmur; ASD: **fixed split S2**, pulmonic flow murmur, RV volume overload
PDA: continuous machinery murmur, bounding pulses; coarctation: weak femoral pulses, arm–leg BP gradient
Central cyanosis: blue lips/tongue, warm extremities → **low arterial saturation**; peripheral: cold extremities

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Left-to-right shunts (VSD, ASD, extracardiac PDA) increase pulmonary flow; remodeling can reverse flow → Eisenmenger syndrome
Duct-dependent lesions require pulmonary/systemic flow or mixing through fetal communications
High neonatal PVR limits VSD shunt → murmur appears/louder over weeks as **PVR falls**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Preductal/right-hand and postductal/foot oxygen saturation; **echocardiography** defines anatomy
★ Hyperoxia test: little PaO2 rise with 100% oxygen suggests cardiac shunting; echo preferred
ECG and chest radiograph support diagnosis; normal murmur does not exclude critical disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected duct-dependent lesion → **prostaglandin E1** immediately; monitor for apnea
★ Tet spell (agitation, softer murmur) → knee–chest, oxygen, fluids, morphine; refractory → phenylephrine or propranolol
TGA with inadequate mixing → balloon atrial septostomy, then arterial switch
Large shunts → diuretics, closure; premature PDA → ibuprofen; **obstructed TAPVR → emergency repair**
Coarctation → repair; post-repair paradoxical hypertension → **IV beta-blocker**; Eisenmenger → **do not close shunt**

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, failure to thrive, arrhythmias, infective endocarditis
Right-to-left shunting → brain abscess, paradoxical emboli, secondary erythrocytosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Pulse-ox newborn screening; rubella immunization before pregnancy; maternal glycemic control
Endocarditis prophylaxis for selected unrepaired cyanotic or prosthetic-material lesions during dental procedures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lung disease: substantial oxygen response, pulmonary findings
PPHN: elevated pulmonary resistance with structurally normal heart

table.title: Five cyanotic lesions
rows: RV obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, RVH; boot-shaped heart
Parallel circuits; single S2; egg-on-string silhouette
Pulmonary veins drain systemically; obstruction → edema

congenital-heart-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric cardiology teaching.

congenital-urinary-tract-anomalies.name: Congenital urinary tract anomalies
congenital-urinary-tract-anomalies.scope: Posterior urethral valves (oligohydramnios, palpable bladder, VCUG, ablation), vesicoureteral reflux (hydronephrosis, recurrent UTI), ureteropelvic junction obstruction, cryptorchidism, hypospadias
congenital-urinary-tract-anomalies.core: Prenatal collecting-system dilation, recurrent febrile UTI, or abnormal genital examination requires localization of obstruction, reflux, or disordered development.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Posterior urethral valves occur only in boys; reflux may cluster in families
Cryptorchidism: prematurity, low birth weight; hypospadias: disrupted urethral development

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Boy with **weak stream, palpable bladder**, bilateral hydronephrosis → outlet obstruction
Severe fetal obstruction → oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, Potter sequence
Recurrent febrile UTIs, poor growth, hypertension may signal reflux nephropathy
★ Hypospadias + bilateral nonpalpable testes → urgent disorder-of-sex-development evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: High urinary pressure or retrograde infected urine damages developing renal parenchyma
Undescended testes experience thermal injury; ectopic ventral meatus may accompany chordee

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Renal/bladder **ultrasound** first; creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis/culture assess consequences
VCUG after abnormal ultrasound suggesting reflux/obstruction or recurrent febrile UTIs; not every first uncomplicated UTI
UPJ dilation without hydroureter → MAG3 diuretic renography for drainage and differential function
Cryptorchidism: examination; no pre-referral ultrasound; bilateral nonpalpable testes → endocrine/genetic evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Valves: bladder catheter decompression, correct fluids/electrolytes → endoscopic **valve ablation**
Reflux: low-risk → observation; high-risk → consider TMP-SMX prophylaxis; breakthrough febrile UTIs → ureteral reimplantation
UPJ obstruction: observe preserved function; worsening drainage/function or symptoms → pyeloplasty
Cryptorchidism: refer at 6 months corrected age; orchiopexy by 18 months
★ Hypospadias: **defer circumcision**; foreskin may support reconstruction; repair generally 6–18 months

rows.label: Complications
items: Renal scarring, CKD, hypertension; valve bladder dysfunction may persist after successful ablation
Cryptorchidism: subfertility, torsion, malignancy; orchiopexy reduces but does not eliminate cancer risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat constipation and dysfunctional voiding to reduce recurrent UTIs
Prompt fever evaluation and long-term BP/renal-function surveillance after significant reflux or obstruction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Retractile testis: can remain in scrotum after manipulation; monitor annually for ascent
Physiologic neonatal dilation: resolves without progressive functional loss

constipation-and-fecal-impaction.name: Constipation and fecal impaction
constipation-and-fecal-impaction.scope: Functional constipation, medication-induced constipation, fecal impaction and overflow incontinence, digital disimpaction, laxatives, fiber
constipation-and-fecal-impaction.core: Difficult, infrequent, or incomplete defecation; loose stool can represent overflow around an impacted rectal stool mass.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Low fiber, immobility, dehydration, withholding, older age; childhood onset often follows painful defecation/toilet training
Opioids, anticholinergics, iron, calcium, verapamil; hypothyroidism, hypercalcemia, neurologic disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Hard/lumpy stool, straining, incomplete emptying, <3 spontaneous stools/week; frequency alone insufficient
★ **Rectal fullness, paradoxical diarrhea, fecal soiling, urinary retention** → consider impaction
★ **Bleeding, anemia, weight loss, new persistent change**, severe distension/vomiting → structural evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Slow transit increases water absorption; pelvic-floor dyssynergia prevents coordinated expulsion
Stool retention stretches rectum → reduced sensation and leakage of liquid around retained mass

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ History, drug review, abdominal examination, **digital rectal examination** for stool, masses, pelvic-floor dysfunction
No alarm findings → clinical diagnosis; targeted TSH/calcium if suspected; colonoscopy for alarms or overdue screening
Refractory despite laxatives → anorectal manometry + balloon-expulsion test; then transit studies if needed
Empty rectum does not exclude proximal impaction; obstruction concern → abdominal imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Palpable hard rectal mass → **manual disimpaction**, then enemas; proximal stool → PEG after obstruction excluded
★ Uncomplicated constipation → **fiber gradually + polyethylene glycol**; hydration if depleted, scheduled postmeal toileting
Dyssynergic defecation → pelvic-floor biofeedback; stool softener alone will not correct outlet dysfunction
Opioid-induced: stimulant + osmotic laxative; refractory → naloxegol/naldemedine after excluding bowel obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Anal fissures, hemorrhoids, prolapse, stercoral ulceration/perforation, recurrent impaction
Magnesium laxatives → hypermagnesemia in CKD; phosphate enemas → electrolyte injury, especially renal disease

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintenance bowel regimen after disimpaction; regular activity, adequate dietary fiber, minimize constipating drugs
Avoid bulk fiber during unresolved impaction; pediatric withholding → reward-based routine, no punishment

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBS-C: recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation/stool changes
Bowel obstruction: colicky pain, vomiting, obstipation, dilated bowel
Hirschsprung: neonatal delayed meconium, distension, absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex

table.title: Escalating agents
rows: Limited efficacy; avoid relying on it

constipation-and-fecal-impaction.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [AGA/ACG constipation guideline 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10544839/); impaction and diagnostic pathways established teaching.

contact-dermatitis.name: Contact dermatitis
contact-dermatitis.scope: Allergic contact dermatitis (poison ivy/urushiol, nickel, neomycin, type IV hypersensitivity), irritant contact dermatitis, patch testing, topical corticosteroids, allergen avoidance
contact-dermatitis.core: Pruritic eczema confined to an exposure pattern; delayed allergy or direct chemical injury, sometimes spreading beyond contact sites.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Allergens: urushiol, nickel jewelry, fragrances, latex additives, neomycin, occupational chemicals
Irritants: repeated handwashing, detergents, solvents, prolonged wet work; atopic skin increases susceptibility
Repeated surgeries, healthcare work → **latex sensitization**

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Linear vesicles** after outdoor exposure; geometric plaques under jewelry, adhesive, or topical products
Acute: erythema, edema, weeping; chronic: fissuring, scaling, lichenification
Irritant disease often burns or stings; allergic disease usually itches
Extensive blistering, facial swelling, genital involvement → assess severity and secondary infection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Allergic: sensitized T cells mediate **type IV hypersensitivity**; symptoms 24–72 hours after re-exposure
Irritant: direct epidermal barrier damage; no prior sensitization required

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical exposure history and distribution first; review work, hobbies, cosmetics, and new skin products
Persistent or unclear allergic disease → **patch testing**, read after delayed intervals
Skin-prick testing and serum IgE do not diagnose delayed contact allergy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Remove exposure → emollients and **topical corticosteroids**; choose potency by body site
Face, groin, folds: low-potency hydrocortisone; thick extremity plaques: triamcinolone
★ Poison ivy **>20% BSA** or severe face/genital disease → oral prednisone taper **2–3 weeks**
Cool wet compresses for oozing; antibiotics only for bacterial superinfection

rows.label: Complications
items: Excoriation → impetigo; persistent exposure → chronic hand eczema and work disability
Prolonged potent topical steroids → skin atrophy, striae; systemic steroids → hyperglycemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Protective gloves and barrier care; fragrance-free products; avoid the identified allergen
Wash urushiol promptly from skin, clothing, and tools; blister fluid does not spread dermatitis
Hand eczema ± generalized urticaria → latex allergy: **strict avoidance**, including intraoperatively; no desensitization

rows.label: Mimics
items: Atopic dermatitis: chronic flexural eczema, personal or family atopy
Tinea: advancing annular scaly border; KOH reveals hyphae
Scabies: nocturnal itch, finger-web burrows, affected close contacts

contact-dermatitis.evidence: Not checked online; established dermatology teaching.

contraception.name: Contraception
contraception.scope: Combined oral contraceptives, progestin-only pills, implant, intrauterine devices, tubal sterilization
contraception.core: Choose contraception through shared decisions about efficacy, bleeding, reversibility, adherence, and estrogen-related vascular risk.

rows.label: Who
items: Anyone seeking pregnancy prevention; adolescents and nulliparous patients can use IUDs or implants
Healthy patient: blood pressure suffices; **no pelvic exam** needed before oral contraceptives

rows.label: Schedule
items: Pills daily; depot medroxyprogesterone every 3 months; implants/IUDs last years (product-dependent)
★ Emergency contraception ≤**5 days**: copper IUD/ulipristal; levonorgestrel ≤72 h, no medical contraindications
Progestin-only pills: daily timing crucial; norethindrone less forgiving than drospirenone

rows.label: Special groups
items: Breastfeeding (estrogen lowers milk volume, protein) or estrogen contraindication → progestin-only or copper IUD
Current breast cancer → copper IUD; avoid hormonal methods
Prior VTE, poor adherence → **IUD/implant** (depot raises VTE risk); older exams: depot, avoid IUD after STI

rows.label: Choice
items: Combined pills: suppress ovulation, improve acne/cramps, reduce endometrial/ovarian cancer risk
★ **LARC** minimizes adherence failures; condoms add STI protection
Tubal sterilization: permanent; counsel regret, alternatives, surgical risk, ectopic risk after failure

rows.label: Contraindications
items: ★ Estrogen: **migraine with aura, prior VTE/thrombophilia**, hypertension (stop pill), early postpartum
Smoking age ≥35: combined methods usually avoid; ≥15 cigarettes/day → absolute contraindication
IUD: pregnancy, cervicitis/PID, distorted cavity (non-distorting fibroid OK); copper: also Wilson disease

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Same-day STI screening need not delay insertion without cervicitis; prior PID alone permits IUD
Sterilization: voluntary informed consent; no required partner approval, parity, or marital status
After ulipristal, wait 5 days before progestin; backup contraception needed after hormonal restart

table.title: Long-acting choices
rows: Treats heavy menses; atrophy → expected benign amenorrhea

dementia.name: Dementia
dementia.scope: Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal, reversible causes, normal cognitive aging vs MCI, Parkinson disease dementia
dementia.core: Acquired cognitive decline interfering with independent daily function; distinguish dementia from normal aging and mild cognitive impairment by functional consequences.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Advanced age: strongest Alzheimer risk; early-onset first-degree family history; Down syndrome (APP triplication)
Vascular risk factors, prior stroke, Parkinson disease
Anticholinergics, sedatives, alcohol, hearing loss, sleep apnea may worsen cognition

rows.label: Clues
items: Collateral history: missed bills/medications, getting lost, unsafe cooking or driving
Personality, language, executive, visuospatial, memory, motor symptoms help establish phenotype
Abrupt change, fluctuating attention, fever, focal deficits → evaluate acute superimposed illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alzheimer: amyloid plaques/tau tangles; Lewy/Parkinson: alpha-synuclein; vascular disease: ischemic neuronal injury
Alzheimer: hippocampal loss → poor delayed/episodic recall; **nucleus basalis of Meynert** loss → acetylcholine deficit
Frontotemporal degeneration affects frontal/anterior temporal networks, often before typical late-life onset

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Patient/informant history, cognition, function**; MoCA/MMSE support diagnosis, cannot establish it alone
★ **CBC, CMP, TSH, B12**, depression/medication review; HIV/syphilis testing if risk
Brain MRI or noncontrast CT → infarcts, mass, subdural, hydrocephalus; avoid routine PET as first test
Normal aging: slower retrieval, preserved independence → reassurance; MCI: objective deficit, independence preserved
Typical Alzheimer: clinical diagnosis after routine labs/imaging; **APOE genotyping not indicated**

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Alzheimer/Lewy/Parkinson dementia → **donepezil or rivastigmine**; moderate/severe Alzheimer → add memantine
Vascular disease → BP/lipid/diabetes control, stroke prevention; frontotemporal behavioral symptoms → consider SSRI
★ Agitation → seek pain/infection, routines/redirection first; **avoid typical antipsychotics in Lewy/Parkinson disease**
Early biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer: specialist-selected antiamyloid drugs; baseline/serial MRI for ARIA
Parkinson dementia psychosis/agitation → **quetiapine** over haloperidol; clozapine needs agranulocytosis monitoring

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, malnutrition, wandering, caregiver burnout; antipsychotics → increased mortality
Cholinesterase inhibitors → bradycardia, syncope, GI effects; antiamyloid antibodies → edema/microhemorrhage
Parkinson disease: dementia strongest predictor of nursing home placement and mortality

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Driving/home safety, advance planning**, caregiver support; assess decision-specific capacity
Visuospatial deficit, e.g., failed pentagon copy → **no car keys** until formal driving assessment
Exercise, hearing correction, social engagement, vascular risk reduction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Delirium: hours–days, impaired attention, fluctuating awareness
Depression: prominent distress, variable effort, potentially reversible cognitive deficits
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus: gait-first decline, incontinence, ventriculomegaly; tap test may predict shunt response

table.title: Phenotype clues
rows: Insidious episodic-memory decline, later multidomain deficits
Stroke-related or stepwise decline, focal findings
Early hallucinations, fluctuation, REM behavior, parkinsonism
Early disinhibition/apathy or progressive aphasia; memory spared
Established motor disease >1 year before dementia

dementia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [Alzheimer's Association diagnostic guidance 2024](https://www.alz.org/news/2024/clinical-practice-guideline-evaluation-alzheimers), [NICE dementia](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng97/chapter/Recommendations/); established subtype teaching.

depressive-disorders.name: Depressive disorders
depressive-disorders.scope: Major depressive disorder criteria, depression in older adults, bereavement vs MDD, pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, suicide risk
depressive-disorders.core: Persistent low mood or loss of pleasure with neurovegetative and cognitive symptoms, causing clinically significant distress or impaired function.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior episodes, family history, chronic illness/pain, substance use, postpartum period, social isolation
Older adults: disability, bereavement, polypharmacy; somatic presentations

rows.label: Clues
items: SIGECAPS: sleep, interest, guilt, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor change, suicidality
Psychotic depression: delusions/hallucinations only during mood episodes, often guilt or nihilism
★ **Suicide risk**: prior attempt, intent, plan, means, agitation, psychosis, intoxication
Youth: **irritable mood** qualifies; academic decline, withdrawal, somatic complaints; not normal teenage behavior

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Multifactorial mood-circuit dysfunction involving monoamines, **HPA hyperactivity with raised cortisol**, and neuroplasticity

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ MDD: **≥5 symptoms for ≥2 weeks**, including depressed mood or anhedonia; exclude mania/hypomania
Screen all adults, even asymptomatic: PHQ-2, PHQ-9 for severity; older adults: **Geriatric Depression Scale**
Interview establishes diagnosis; assess substances, drugs, TSH/CBC when clinically suspected
★ **Ask directly about suicide**, access to firearms, protective factors; questioning does not increase risk
Post-CABG anhedonia, withdrawal, fatigue → depression screen; vein-harvest leg edema expected

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Imminent danger or **severe malnutrition** → **observation, psychiatric hospitalization**; remove lethal means
Mild: CBT/interpersonal therapy; moderate/severe: sertraline + psychotherapy; pregnancy → shared risk–benefit discussion
★ Urgent suicidality/catatonia/anorexia → **ECT**; psychotic depression → ECT or antidepressant + antipsychotic
Alternatives: **bupropion** (fatigue/hypersomnia, smoking cessation), **mirtazapine** (poor appetite, insomnia)
Continue antidepressant ≥6 months after remission; recurrent/severe episodes → longer maintenance

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, malnutrition, functional decline, recurrence
SSRIs: sexual dysfunction, GI effects, hyponatremia; early activation/suicidality monitoring, especially age <25
Bupropion: seizures; avoid with eating disorders, seizure disorders or brain tumor; mirtazapine: weight gain/sedation
Benzodiazepines in older adults: worsen depression, sedation, falls → stop, use antidepressant

rows.label: Prevention
items: Safety plan, early follow-up after drug changes
Taper antidepressants to reduce discontinuation symptoms; avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder

rows.label: Mimics
items: Dementia: insidious consistent deficits; **pseudodementia**: subacute, "I don't know" answers, recall improves with prompting
Hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, constipation, elevated TSH
Untreated OSA: snoring, obesity, sleepiness → **mood disorder due to medical condition**, not MDD
Anorexia nervosa: fear of weight gain, distorted body image

table.title: Distinguishing persistent sadness
rows: Waves tied to reminders; self-esteem usually preserved
Pervasive worthlessness; bereavement does not exclude diagnosis
Stressor within 3 months; MDD criteria absent

diabetic-neuropathy.name: Diabetic neuropathy
diabetic-neuropathy.scope: Distal symmetric polyneuropathy, autonomic neuropathy, mononeuropathy, foot ulcer prevention, pharmacotherapy (duloxetine, pregabalin, TCAs)
diabetic-neuropathy.core: Diabetes damages sensory, motor, and autonomic nerves; identify the pattern, exclude additional causes, relieve pain, and protect insensate feet.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Long diabetes duration, chronic hyperglycemia, smoking, kidney disease, dyslipidemia
Alcohol excess and metformin-associated B12 deficiency may coexist and worsen symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Acute asymmetric weakness, marked motor loss**, or rapid progression → investigate another cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Metabolic and microvascular injury damages peripheral axons; longest nerves affected first
Loss of protective sensation plus deformity/ischemia → repetitive unnoticed trauma

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **10-g monofilament + vibration/pinprick/temperature**, ankle reflexes; inspect skin, deformity, pulses
Screen at type 2 diagnosis, 5 years after type 1 diagnosis, then at least annually
Check B12, TSH, renal function when evaluating neuropathy; consider serum electrophoresis if unexplained
Atypical pattern → nerve conduction studies; gastroparesis → exclude obstruction, gastric-emptying study
New third-nerve palsy → urgent vascular imaging; pupil sparing cannot reliably exclude aneurysm

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pain → **duloxetine or pregabalin**; gabapentin or TCAs (nortriptyline, amitriptyline) alternatives
Avoid TCAs with arrhythmia, urinary retention, frailty; avoid opioids for routine chronic neuropathic pain
Improve glycemic management; no drug reliably restores established sensory loss
Orthostasis → hydration, compression, medication review; persistent symptoms → midodrine
Gastroparesis → small low-fat meals, short-term metoclopramide; erectile dysfunction → sildenafil unless nitrates

rows.label: Complications
items: Painless ulcers, osteomyelitis, amputation, Charcot arthropathy
Falls, burns, painless MI; metoclopramide → tardive dyskinesia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Daily foot inspection, protective footwear**, podiatry for callus/nail care; never walk barefoot
Regular foot exams, smoking cessation; warm swollen neuropathic foot → off-load and assess Charcot/infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: B12 deficiency: posterior column findings, elevated methylmalonic acid
Lumbar disc radiculopathy: back pain radiating down leg, root-specific weakness
Peripheral arterial disease: exertional pain, reduced pulses, ischemic skin changes

diabetic-neuropathy.evidence: Not checked online; established diabetes neuropathy screening and management teaching.

table.title: Clinical patterns
rows: Burning/numb feet, reduced vibration and ankle reflexes
Orthostasis, tachycardia, gastroparesis, bladder/sexual dysfunction, hypoglycemia unawareness
Acute isolated nerve deficit; often reversible
Unilateral belt-like burning pain, one truncal dermatome

diagnostic-test-accuracy.name: Diagnostic test accuracy
diagnostic-test-accuracy.scope: Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, likelihood ratios, cut-off changes
diagnostic-test-accuracy.core: Diagnostic accuracy: classification performance against a reference standard; distinguish detection ability from the probability that a result reflects disease.

rows.label: Definition
items: TP/FP: diseased/nondiseased testing positive; FN/TN: diseased/nondiseased testing negative
False negatives → low sensitivity, an intrinsic test property; NPV varies with prevalence

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ ↑Prevalence → **↑PPV, ↓NPV**; sensitivity/specificity unchanged if disease spectrum unchanged
★ Positive above threshold: **lower cutoff → ↑sensitivity, ↓specificity**; raising cutoff reverses
LR+ >10 rules in; LR− <0.1 rules out; **LR 1** → no information

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ Pretest odds = p/(1−p); **posttest odds = pretest odds × LR**
Posttest probability = odds/(1+odds); pretest 20%, LR+ 4 → odds 1 → 50%
Parallel tests, either positive → ↑sensitivity; serial tests, both positive → ↑specificity

rows.label: Compare
items: ROC: sensitivity versus 1−specificity; AUC 0.5 = chance, 1 = perfect
ROC point nearest **upper-left corner** → best combined sensitivity and specificity

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Sensitive negative** helps exclude; specific positive helps confirm; neither absolute
Case-control sampling → PPV/NPV unrepresentative without population prevalence
Verification bias: reference testing only selected results → distorted accuracy

diagnostic-test-accuracy.evidence: Established statistical definitions; no guideline-dependent recommendation.

dyslipidemia.name: Dyslipidemia
dyslipidemia.scope: Lipid screening guidelines, ASCVD risk calculation, statin therapy indications, monitoring response to diet and pharmacotherapy
dyslipidemia.core: Excess atherogenic lipoproteins drive ASCVD; treatment intensity follows established disease, severe LDL elevation, diabetes, and estimated absolute cardiovascular risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Familial disorders, saturated-fat intake, obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis
Premature ASCVD family history, CKD, smoking, inflammatory disease increase treatment benefit

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually asymptomatic; tendon xanthomas/early corneal arcus suggest familial hypercholesterolemia
Severe triglyceride elevation: eruptive xanthomas, pancreatitis; low HDL alone is not a drug target

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Retained apoB-containing particles → arterial inflammation and plaque formation
Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → hepatic LDL-receptor upregulation
Familial hypercholesterolemia: **defective LDL-receptor uptake** → isolated high LDL, clear plasma; high TG: milky plasma

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Lipid panel from age 19, at least every 5 years**; earlier/more often with risk
Nonfasting panel acceptable; markedly high triglycerides → fasting repeat/secondary-cause evaluation; Lp(a) once/lifetime
★ **PREVENT-ASCVD**, ages 30–79, LDL 70–189 without ASCVD: replaces pooled-cohort equations in 2026 guidance
Uncertain statin decision → coronary calcium; zero insufficient for deferral with diabetes, smoking, strong premature history
High total cholesterol alone → full lipid panel before treatment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Clinical ASCVD (CAD, stroke, PAD) or **LDL ≥190 mg/dL → high-intensity statin**, no risk calculation required
★ Diabetes age 40–75 → **at least moderate-intensity statin**; multiple risk factors favor high intensity
Above LDL target despite maximal statin → ezetimibe; consider PCSK9 inhibitor or bempedoic acid
Severe triglycerides ≥500 → address causes, diet, consider fenofibrate/prescription omega-3 to reduce pancreatitis risk
Adolescent obesity + moderate LDL → **calorie reduction/lifestyle first**; statin only if severe or persistent

rows.label: Complications
items: MI, stroke, peripheral arterial disease; statins → myalgias, rare rhabdomyolysis, small diabetes-risk increase
Baseline ALT; CK only with symptoms/risk; most lipid-lowering drugs deferred during conception/pregnancy/lactation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Mediterranean-style diet, replace saturated fats, exercise, weight reduction, smoking cessation
★ Recheck lipids **4–12 weeks after diet/drug change**, then every 3–12 months; high despite diet → statin
High intensity lowers LDL ≥50%: atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypothyroidism: elevated TSH; correct before labeling primary dyslipidemia
Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia; treat renal cause

table.title: Risk-based primary prevention and secondary target

dysmenorrhea.name: Dysmenorrhea
dysmenorrhea.scope: Primary dysmenorrhea, secondary dysmenorrhea (endometriosis, adenomyosis, cervical stenosis), hematometra, NSAIDs, combined oral contraceptives
dysmenorrhea.core: Painful menstruation: primary disease begins after ovulatory cycles develop; later-onset, progressive, or refractory pain suggests pelvic pathology.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Early menarche, heavy/prolonged flow, family history, smoking
Prior cervical excision/ablation → stenosis; endometriosis and adenomyosis produce secondary symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Suprapubic cramping radiating to back/thighs, nausea, diarrhea, headache
★ **Dyspareunia, abnormal bleeding, infertility**, or pain outside menses → secondary cause
Amenorrhea or scant flow after cervical procedure with cyclic pain → retained menstrual blood

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Progesterone withdrawal → endometrial prostaglandins → uterine hypercontractility and ischemia
Outflow obstruction traps blood in uterine cavity → hematometra

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Classic adolescent presentation without red flags → **clinical diagnosis**, no initial imaging
Sexual activity → pregnancy test; infection risks → gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT
Secondary features → pelvic examination and **transvaginal ultrasound**; transabdominal imaging if needed
No improvement after 3–6 months despite adherence → investigate secondary disease, consider laparoscopy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NSAIDs**, starting 1–2 days before expected bleeding through first 2–3 days
★ Inadequate response/contraception desired → **combined OCP** or progestin; continuous suppression may help
Heat, exercise; avoid NSAIDs with active ulcer disease or significant renal dysfunction
Treat underlying lesion; cervical stenosis with hematometra → cervical dilation/drainage

rows.label: Complications
items: School/work absence, sleep disturbance; untreated secondary disease may impair fertility
Analgesic adverse effects: GI bleeding, renal injury; estrogen-containing contraception → VTE risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Track cycles and preempt pain; ongoing menstrual suppression reduces recurrence when pregnancy not desired

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ectopic pregnancy: positive hCG, nonmenstrual bleeding, possible instability
PID: fever, mucopurulent discharge, cervical motion tenderness

table.title: Secondary patterns
rows: Posterior nodularity; ultrasound may be normal
Heavy bleeding, boggy uniformly enlarged uterus

dysmenorrhea.evidence: Not checked online; established adolescent gynecology and pelvic-pain teaching.

dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.name: Dyspepsia and peptic ulcer disease
dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.scope: Uninvestigated dyspepsia (age < 60 test-and-treat vs age >= 60 endoscopy), Helicobacter pylori testing and eradication, gastric and duodenal ulcers
dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.core: Epigastric discomfort may reflect functional dyspepsia or acid-peptic ulceration; age and bleeding risk determine noninvasive testing versus endoscopy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: H pylori, NSAIDs/aspirin; smoking impairs healing
Prior ulcer bleeding, anticoagulants, older age amplify NSAID harm; severe physiologic stress causes ICU ulcers

rows.label: Clues
items: Epigastric burning, early satiety, nausea; meal timing cannot reliably distinguish ulcer location
★ **Alarm**: hematemesis/melena, positive occult blood, dysphagia, persistent vomiting, weight loss, iron-deficiency anemia
Sudden rigid abdomen → perforation
Early satiety, nonbilious vomiting, succussion splash, gastric distention → gastric outlet obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: H pylori or prostaglandin depletion weakens mucosal defenses against acid-pepsin injury
Antral-predominant infection increases acid; corpus-predominant inflammation may cause atrophy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ New dyspepsia **≥60 years or any alarm feature → upper endoscopy**
★ Under 60 without concerning features → **urea breath or stool antigen test**
Hold PPI 2 weeks and antibiotics/bismuth 4 weeks before active-infection testing; serology cannot confirm eradication
Gastric ulcer → biopsy to exclude malignancy; duodenal ulcers rarely malignant
Refractory/recurrent multiple ulcers + diarrhea → fasting gastrin with careful PPI interpretation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ H pylori → **14-day bismuth quadruple**: PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole
Avoid empiric clarithromycin/levofloxacin regimens unless susceptibility demonstrated
Negative infection test or persistent symptoms after eradication → PPI trial; functional symptoms may need TCA
Stop NSAID; ulcer healing → PPI; active bleeding → resuscitation, IV PPI, urgent endoscopic hemostasis
Perforation → IV fluids, ceftriaxone/metronidazole, urgent surgery; no elective diagnostic endoscopy

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhage, perforation, penetration, outlet obstruction from scarring/fibrosis; H pylori → gastric cancer, MALT lymphoma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Confirm eradication ≥4 weeks after antibiotics** with breath/stool test, off PPI as above
Necessary NSAID + high GI risk → concurrent PPI; use lowest effective NSAID exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Biliary colic: episodic RUQ pain, gallstones on ultrasound
ACS: exertional epigastric pressure, ischemic ECG/troponin findings

dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG H pylori update (2024)](https://gi.org/journals-publications/ebgi/schoenfeld_sep2024/); dyspepsia age threshold established ACG/CAG teaching.

early-pregnancy-loss.name: Early pregnancy loss
early-pregnancy-loss.scope: Threatened abortion, inevitable abortion, incomplete abortion, complete abortion, missed abortion, anembryonic pregnancy
early-pregnancy-loss.core: First-trimester bleeding requires pregnancy location and viability assessment before labeling miscarriage or choosing expectant, medical, or surgical management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Embryonic aneuploidy most common; maternal age, prior losses, uterine anomalies, antiphospholipid syndrome

rows.label: Clues
items: Cramping, vaginal bleeding, passage of tissue; symptoms may be absent with retained nonviable pregnancy
★ Hypotension, syncope, peritoneal signs → **hemorrhage or ruptured ectopic**
Fever, uterine tenderness, foul discharge → septic abortion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Embryonic/fetal demise or failed embryonic development → decidual separation and variable cervical dilation
Corpus luteum progesterone sustains pregnancy until ~10 weeks; removal earlier → **progesterone supplementation**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Transvaginal ultrasound** plus quantitative β-hCG; CBC, blood type, pelvic examination
Definitive nonviability: CRL ≥7 mm without heartbeat or mean sac diameter ≥25 mm without embryo
Absent embryo/heartbeat on repeat: ≥11 days after yolk sac, ≥14 days after sac-only → nonviable
No intrauterine pregnancy → serial hCG/ultrasound; tissue passage alone cannot exclude ectopic

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable, infected, or uncontrolled hemorrhage → **urgent uterine aspiration**; sepsis → IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
Confirmed stable loss → patient choice: observation, mifepristone followed by misoprostol, or aspiration
Threatened loss → expectant follow-up; bed rest does not prevent miscarriage
Stable, unlocated pregnancy, falling hCG → serial hCG until negative; no methotrexate
★ Rh-negative loss **≥12 weeks → RhIg**; ACOG omits routine testing earlier; older exam questions may expect Rh typing

rows.label: Complications
items: Retained products, infection, hemorrhage; intrauterine adhesions after instrumentation; grief/depression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking/alcohol avoidance, optimize diabetes; most isolated chromosomal losses unpreventable
Recurrent clinical losses → assess uterine anatomy, antiphospholipid antibodies and selected genetic causes

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ectopic pregnancy: extrauterine implantation, adnexal mass/free fluid
Gestational trophoblastic disease: very high hCG, abnormal cystic intrauterine tissue
Subchorionic hematoma: bleeding without cramping; viable intrauterine pregnancy, perichorionic collection
Normal early pregnancy: spotting, 5-week sac, hCG ~1,000, simple corpus luteum cyst; embryo not yet expected

eating-disorders.name: Eating disorders
eating-disorders.scope: Anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder, refeeding syndrome, medical complications, hospitalization criteria
eating-disorders.core: Disordered intake or compensatory behaviors require assessment of medical instability, suicidality, and malnutrition at any body size.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Adolescence, dieting, weight stigma, perfectionism, trauma; psychiatric comorbidity and family history

rows.label: Clues
items: Restrictive disease: cold intolerance, lanugo, bradycardia, orthostasis, menstrual suppression; amenorrhea not required
Purging: parotid hypertrophy, **raised amylase**, enamel erosion, knuckle calluses; hypokalemic hypochloremic alkalosis
★ **Syncope, arrhythmia, hypothermia or severe electrolyte abnormalities** → urgent stabilization

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Starvation suppresses gonadal axis and reduces cardiac mass; vomiting causes chloride/volume depletion
Refeeding insulin surge shifts phosphate, potassium and magnesium intracellularly

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical interview plus weight trajectory, vitals/orthostatics, **ECG, electrolytes, Mg, phosphate**
Binge: loss of control plus unusually large intake; bulimia/BED require episodes ≥weekly for 3 months
Assess suicide risk, substance use, exercise, laxatives; normal BMI does not exclude severe disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Medical admission for instability: e.g., HR <50, BP <90/60, severe electrolyte disturbance or acute food refusal
★ Refeeding → **thiamine**, nutritional rehabilitation, serial phosphate/K/Mg and cardiac monitoring
Adolescent anorexia → family-based treatment; adults → eating-disorder-focused psychotherapy; medication alone insufficient
Bulimia → CBT plus fluoxetine; avoid bupropion because of seizures
BED → CBT; lisdexamfetamine for selected adults, monitor misuse/cardiovascular risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoestrogenism → osteoporosis, infertility; cardiac failure, arrhythmic death; purging → arrhythmias, esophageal injury
Refeeding → hypophosphatemia, respiratory failure, edema, delirium; high suicide mortality
Severe starvation → **hypoalbuminemia** with pitting edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early recognition of growth/weight-trajectory changes; reduce weight-based stigma; relapse follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperthyroidism: increased appetite with tremor and heat intolerance
GI malabsorption: involuntary weight loss without weight/shape-driven restriction

eating-disorders.evidence: Guideline framework checked 2026-10-30: [APA eating disorders guideline, 2023](https://www.psychiatry.org/psychiatrists/practice/clinical-practice-guidelines/eating-disorders); thresholds: established clinical teaching.

table.title: Diagnostic distinction
rows: Restriction or purging + weight-gain fear/distorted self-image

elder-abuse-and-neglect.name: Elder abuse and neglect
elder-abuse-and-neglect.scope: Physical abuse, psychological abuse, neglect, financial exploitation, clinical red flags, reporting to adult protective services
elder-abuse-and-neglect.core: Unexplained injury, unmet basic needs, intimidation, or loss of financial control warrants private assessment, safety planning, and mandated reporting.

rows.label: Principle
items: Respect autonomy while protecting vulnerable adults; decision-making capacity is specific to the decision
Dependence, cognitive impairment, isolation, caregiver strain, and coercion increase vulnerability
Genital laceration/bleeding in dependent elder → suspect sexual abuse

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Interview separately**; ask about safety, threats, caregiving, finances, basic needs
★ Stabilize injuries; assess cognition, capacity, suicidality, immediate danger, and safe disposition
★ Document quotes/findings; report suspected abuse to **Adult Protective Services**

rows.label: Don't
items: Do not confront the suspected abuser before arranging safety or disclose confidential plans unnecessarily
Do not require proof, a confession, or patient permission when reporting is legally mandatory
Poverty, accidental bruises, informed treatment refusal alone → insufficient evidence of neglect

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Immediate danger → emergency services; suspected crime may require police reporting
Capacitated adult can usually decline services; mandatory reporting may still apply under state law
Incapacity with unsafe care → protective intervention, surrogate review, possible emergency guardianship

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Inconsistent histories, different injury ages**, delayed care, controlling caregiver → investigate
Malnutrition, pressure injuries, medication deprivation → neglect; forced signatures → exploitation
Psychological abuse may leave no physical marks; arrange social work and confidential follow-up

elder-abuse-and-neglect.evidence: Not checked online; established ethics principles; reporting statutes vary by jurisdiction.

epistaxis.name: Epistaxis
epistaxis.scope: Anterior epistaxis (Kiesselbach plexus), posterior epistaxis (sphenopalatine artery), risk factors (arid climate, digital trauma, hypertension), direct pressure, topical vasoconstrictors, nasal packing, chemical cautery
epistaxis.core: Anterior septal bleeding predominates; ongoing blood in the throat suggests a posterior source.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Dry air, digital trauma, nasal sprays or surgery; anticoagulation and bleeding disorders prolong bleeding
Older age and hypertension associated with more severe or posterior bleeding

rows.label: Clues
items: Anterior: usually visible unilateral source; posterior: brisk bleeding from both nares
★ Airway compromise, tachycardia or hypotension → major hemorrhage

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Superficial mucosal vessels vulnerable to drying and minor trauma; posterior arterial bleeding can be brisk

rows.label: Dx
items: Clear clots then anterior rhinoscopy; recurrent unilateral or refractory bleeding → nasal endoscopy
Severe or recurrent bleeding → CBC; coagulation studies when anticoagulated or coagulopathy suspected

rows.label: Tx
items: Unstable → airway protection, IV access and resuscitation
★ Lean forward and pinch soft nose ≥5 minutes uninterrupted; topical oxymetazoline if persistent
★ Visible anterior source → **silver nitrate** after local anesthesia; avoid bilateral septal cautery
Persistent unseen source → pack; use resorbable material with antithrombotics or bleeding disorder
★ Posterior packing → ENT and monitored admission; refractory → ligation or embolization

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, anemia or shock; packing can cause pressure necrosis; septal cautery can cause perforation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Humidification, saline gel, avoid picking and forceful nose blowing after bleeding

rows.label: Mimics
items: Upper GI bleeding: hematemesis or melena without nasal source
Hemoptysis: blood coughed up with lower respiratory symptoms and no nasal source

epistaxis.evidence: Checked AAO-HNSF Nosebleed clinical practice guideline (2020).

esophageal-motility-disorders.name: Esophageal motility disorders
esophageal-motility-disorders.scope: Achalasia, diffuse esophageal spasm, hypercontractile esophagus, Zenker diverticulum, manometry, barium swallow
esophageal-motility-disorders.core: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from onset suggests impaired motility; progressive solids-first dysphagia suggests mechanical obstruction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Achalasia often idiopathic; Chagas disease can destroy enteric ganglia
Older age predisposes to Zenker diverticulum; opioids can produce spastic motility patterns

rows.label: Clues
items: Achalasia: regurgitated undigested food, nocturnal cough, weight loss
★ Zenker: **halitosis, cervical gurgling, aspiration**, retained food hours after eating
Spastic disorders: intermittent dysphagia and squeezing chest pain; hot/cold liquids may provoke

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Achalasia: loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons → impaired LES relaxation and absent peristalsis
Zenker: cricopharyngeal dysfunction → mucosal herniation through Killian triangle

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Esophageal symptoms → **upper endoscopy** to exclude stricture/cancer before motility testing
★ **High-resolution manometry** confirms functional disorder after structural disease excluded
Barium swallow defines emptying; suspected Zenker → **barium study before endoscopy**
Rapid weight loss, older onset or difficult LES passage → evaluate pseudoachalasia with CT/endoscopic ultrasound
Chest pain → exclude ACS before labeling esophageal spasm

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Achalasia → pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy + fundoplication, or **POEM**
Botulinum toxin for achalasia when procedural risk precludes durable treatment
Spastic disorders → remove opioid trigger, treat reflux; diltiazem or nitrates for persistent symptoms
Symptomatic Zenker → **cricopharyngeal myotomy + diverticulectomy** or endoscopic septotomy; no dilation or blind NG tube

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition; longstanding achalasia → increased squamous cancer risk
Dilation/myotomy → perforation; myotomy, especially POEM → gastroesophageal reflux

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eat slowly, chew thoroughly, remain upright after meals to reduce regurgitation/aspiration

rows.label: Mimics
items: Esophageal cancer: progressive solids-first symptoms; obstructing lesion
Scleroderma: hypotensive LES with reflux, distal aperistalsis

table.title: Manometry and contrast findings
rows: Impaired LES relaxation; absent normal peristalsis

esophageal-motility-disorders.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG achalasia guideline](https://gi.org/guideline/diagnosis-and-management-of-achalasia/); other disorders established teaching.

esophageal-perforation.name: Esophageal perforation
esophageal-perforation.scope: Boerhaave syndrome, iatrogenic perforation, mediastinitis, gastrografin esophagography, emergent surgical repair
esophageal-perforation.core: Severe chest pain after vomiting or esophageal instrumentation, with systemic toxicity or mediastinal air, is an esophageal emergency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Endoscopy, dilation, foreign bodies, caustic injury; forceful emesis causes spontaneous Boerhaave rupture
Underlying stricture or malignancy increases instrumentation-related injury risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachycardia, fever, dyspnea, odynophagia; neck swelling or palpable crepitus
★ **Left pleural effusion**, pneumomediastinum or subcutaneous emphysema after retching
Hypotension, rising lactate, organ dysfunction → uncontrolled contamination and sepsis
Classic vomiting–pain–emphysema triad often incomplete; absence does not exclude rupture

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Full-thickness tear releases saliva, gastric contents and bacteria into mediastinum/pleura
Boerhaave typically affects distal posterolateral esophagus; contamination causes chemical then infectious mediastinitis

rows.label: Dx
items: **Upright chest x-ray first** for mediastinal/pleural air; normal early film does not exclude → contrast study
★ Stable suspected leak → **CT chest with water-soluble oral contrast** or water-soluble esophagram
Gastrografin study negative with persistent suspicion → thin barium study to detect small leaks
Avoid routine diagnostic endoscopy when insufflation could enlarge an uncontained tear

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO**, IV fluids, IV piperacillin–tazobactam, urgent thoracic/general surgery consultation
★ Free pleural/mediastinal leak (even stable) or shock → **operative repair + drainage**; chest tube inadequate
Contained leak without sepsis → antibiotics, drainage ± endoscopic closure/stent; older questions may expect surgery
IV proton-pump inhibitor; enteral feeding distal to leak or parenteral nutrition
Avoid blind nasogastric placement; decompression, if needed, under specialist guidance

rows.label: Complications
items: Mediastinitis, empyema, septic shock, multiorgan failure; delay markedly worsens outcomes
Persistent fistula, esophageal stricture and malnutrition after healing

rows.label: Prevention
items: Careful procedural technique; prompt evaluation of new pain following esophageal instrumentation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mallory–Weiss: mucosal tear causing hematemesis without mediastinal contamination
ACS: ischemic ECG/troponin pattern; no contrast leak
Acute aortic syndrome: vascular abnormality on CT angiography

esophageal-perforation.evidence: Not checked online; established emergency esophageal management.

essential-hypertension.name: Essential hypertension
essential-hypertension.scope: Blood pressure staging, nonpharmacologic interventions (weight loss, DASH, exercise), first-line antihypertensive agents, resistant hypertension
essential-hypertension.core: Persistently elevated arterial pressure usually reflects multifactorial primary hypertension; confirm accurate repeated measurements before long-term treatment decisions.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, family history, obesity, excess sodium/alcohol, inactivity, poor sleep
NSAIDs, stimulants, oral contraceptives can raise BP; assess before labeling primary disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually asymptomatic; headache alone does not establish hypertensive emergency
★ **Acute target-organ injury** with severe pressure → hypertensive emergency; BP number alone insufficient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased vascular resistance, altered renal sodium handling, sympathetic/RAAS activation sustain elevated pressure
Chronic endothelial injury accelerates atherosclerosis and small-vessel organ damage
Older adults: large-artery stiffness (low compliance) → **isolated systolic hypertension**, wide pulse pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Average ≥2 readings on ≥2 visits; confirm using **home BP or ambulatory monitoring**
Rest seated, feet supported, correct cuff, arm at heart level; avoid recent caffeine/exercise
BMP, creatinine/eGFR, urinalysis/albuminuria, lipids, glucose/A1c, ECG assess risk and injury
Resistant: above goal on 3 agents including diuretic, or controlled on ≥4; exclude pseudoresistance
Child/adolescent high oscillometric reading → **confirm by auscultation** before ambulatory monitoring or workup

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **DASH diet, weight reduction, sodium restriction, aerobic activity**, moderate alcohol; target generally <130/80
≥140/90 → drugs, usually two classes; ≥130/80 with CVD, diabetes, CKD, or PREVENT ≥7.5% → drugs
★ Low-risk stage 1: **3–6 months lifestyle**, then drugs if still ≥130/80; updated 2025 threshold
Initial: chlorthalidone, amlodipine, lisinopril, or losartan; albuminuric CKD → ACE inhibitor/ARB (older exams: any diabetes)
Resistant after optimized triple regimen → spironolactone; monitor K/creatinine; never combine ACE inhibitor + ARB

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, MI, LV hypertrophy/HF, CKD, retinopathy, aortic disease
Thiazide: low Na/K, gout; ACE inhibitor: cough/angioedema; RAAS drugs contraindicated in pregnancy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication adherence, home readings, regular follow-up; assess orthostatic symptoms in older adults
Weight loss: largest lifestyle BP drop, ~1 mm Hg/kg; smoking cessation barely lowers resting BP
BP control: largest modifiable stroke-risk reduction; also prevents concentric LVH and HF

rows.label: Mimics
